title: Handling a Facebook account after death: a Sydney family guide
excerpt: Learn how to manage a loved one's Facebook account after death. Secure their accounts, gather necessary documents, and make informed decisions.
content:
![Hands holding phone beside memorial candle](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1786202125458_Hands-holding-phone-beside-memorial-candle.jpeg)

When someone you love passes away, their Facebook account and online presence need attention quickly. Three actions matter most: secure any shared devices and financial accounts linked to their email to prevent fraud, gather a certified copy of the death certificate and any executor or probate papers, and decide whether to memorialise, appoint a legacy contact, or permanently delete the Facebook account before submitting a platform request to Meta. The [eSafety Commissioner advises families](https://www.esafety.gov.au/key-topics/digital-wellbeing/what-happens-to-your-digital-accounts-after-you-die/) to treat these security steps as urgent, not optional.

- **Secure accounts now.** Change passwords on any shared email or streaming accounts, freeze digital banking where possible, and remove saved payment details from shared devices.
- **Gather documents.** A certified death certificate, proof of your relationship or executor authority, and an obituary link or news article are the documents most platforms require.
- **Choose a Facebook option.** Memorialise the account, activate a pre-nominated legacy contact, or request permanent deletion through Meta's special request form.

**Pro Tip:** *If the deceased nominated a legacy contact inside Facebook's settings before they passed, that person can act immediately without waiting for probate. Check Settings > Memorialisation Settings first.*

***

## Key takeaways

Managing a deceased person's Facebook account requires three immediate actions: securing shared devices and financial accounts, gathering documents, and submitting the correct Meta platform request within the first 72 hours.

| Point | Details |
|---|---|
| Secure accounts first | Change shared passwords and freeze digital banking before addressing social media. |
| Documents to have ready | Certified death certificate, proof of executor authority or relationship, and an obituary link. |
| Three Meta options | Memorialise, activate a legacy contact (if pre-set), or request permanent deletion via Meta's online form. |
| Legal limits in Australia | No national law governs platform access; executors cannot log in or read private messages without a court order. |
| Willow Tree Funerals | Bruce Missen provides 24/7 personal support for obituary wording, memorial notices, and funeral arrangements across Sydney. |

***

## Table of Contents

- [What to do in the first 72 hours after a death](#what-to-do-in-the-first-72-hours-after-a-death)
- [How Facebook and Instagram handle accounts after a death](#how-facebook-and-instagram-handle-accounts-after-a-death)
- [What executors and family can and can't do under Australian law](#what-executors-and-family-can-and-cant-do-under-australian-law)
- [How to create a digital inventory and appoint a digital executor](#how-to-create-a-digital-inventory-and-appoint-a-digital-executor)
- [How to preserve photos, videos and messages from a Facebook account](#how-to-preserve-photos-videos-and-messages-from-a-facebook-account)
- [What to do when you can't access the Facebook account](#what-to-do-when-you-cant-access-the-facebook-account)
- [How to protect the family from scams and identity theft after a death](#how-to-protect-the-family-from-scams-and-identity-theft-after-a-death)
- [Managing other social media platforms and online services](#managing-other-social-media-platforms-and-online-services)
- [How long does Facebook memorialisation or deletion take?](#how-long-does-facebook-memorialisation-or-deletion-take)
- [How to contact Facebook support for a deceased person's account](#how-to-contact-facebook-support-for-a-deceased-persons-account)
- [Willow Tree Funerals: practical support for memorial notices and online legacy](#willow-tree-funerals-practical-support-for-memorial-notices-and-online-legacy)
- [Sources](#sources)
- [FAQ](#faq)

## What to do in the first 72 hours after a death

Acting quickly reduces the risk of identity theft and account misuse. Work through these steps in order.

**First 24 hours**

1. Secure bank cards and freeze digital banking through the relevant financial institution.
2. Change passwords on any shared household accounts (email, streaming, utilities).
3. Obtain at least two certified copies of the death certificate from the attending doctor or hospital.
4. Note down every social media platform and email address you are aware of.

**24–72 hours**

5. Log a basic digital inventory: account names, usernames, and whether you have login details.
6. Check Facebook's Memorialisation Settings to see whether a legacy contact was nominated.
7. Contact Meta through its Special Request for Deceased Person's Account form to begin memorialisation or deletion.
8. Notify close friends and family so they can watch for scam messages sent from the account before it is secured.

According to [practical estate administration guidance](https://www.thesenior.com.au/story/9147265/what-happens-to-your-social-media-when-you-die-australian-guide/), families should avoid logging into the deceased's accounts without executor authority unless there is an immediate security concern, as unauthorised access can complicate estate administration later.

**Pro Tip:** *Security actions (freezing bank accounts, changing shared passwords) can be taken by any immediate family member. Estate administration actions (requesting deletion, downloading archives) should wait for the executor unless urgency demands otherwise.*

***

## How Facebook and Instagram handle accounts after a death

Meta offers three distinct paths for a deceased person's account. Understanding what each allows will help you choose the right one.

![Comparison diagram of Facebook account management options](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1786202716150_Comparison-diagram-of-Facebook-account-management-options.jpeg)

**Memorialisation** converts the profile into a memorial space. The word "Remembering" appears beside the person's name, no one can log in, and private messages remain inaccessible. Friends and family can still post tributes on the timeline. [Law Reform NSW confirms](https://lawreform.nsw.gov.au/documents/Publications/Consultation-Papers/CP20.pdf) that legacy contacts can manage memorialised profiles but cannot read private messages.

**Legacy contact** is a person the account holder nominates in advance inside Facebook's settings. They can pin a tribute post, respond to new friend requests, and, if the account holder permitted it, download a copy of the account's data. They cannot log in as the deceased, read private messages, or remove existing posts.

**Permanent deletion** removes the account entirely. This can be requested by an immediate family member or verified executor. Meta requires a death certificate and proof of relationship or authority.

Instagram, also owned by Meta, follows the same process through its own Special Request form.

**Pro Tip:** *If the deceased never nominated a legacy contact, you can still request memorialisation or deletion. You simply cannot retroactively appoint one after death.*

***

## What executors and family can and can't do under Australian law

[Australia currently has no single national law](https://www.coulterlegal.com.au/what-happens-to-my-social-media-accounts-when-i-die-and-why-should-i-care/) governing access to a deceased person's online accounts. Platform Terms of Service and case-by-case legal advice fill the gap, which means your rights depend largely on what each platform chooses to allow.

**What executors can generally do:**

- Submit memorialisation or deletion requests with supporting documents.
- Request a data archive if the account holder pre-authorised it via a legacy contact.
- Provide a death certificate, executor papers, and proof of relationship to support requests.

**What executors typically cannot do without a court order:**

- Log into the account directly.
- Read private messages or access encrypted content.
- Transfer account ownership or monetisation rights to a beneficiary.

> Executors should be aware that many digital assets are governed by licences, not ownership. As [KKI Lawyers explain](https://kkilawyers.com.au/who-owns-your-digital-legacy-when-you-die/), a Will may not be sufficient to grant access to certain online accounts because the licence ends at death. For accounts with genuine commercial value, specialist legal advice is usually necessary.

Documents platforms commonly require: a certified death certificate, proof of executor authority or letters of administration, proof of relationship (birth or marriage certificate), and an obituary link or published death notice. See the documents guide from Willow Tree Funerals for a practical checklist of what to prepare.

**Pro Tip:** *Where an account has commercial value (a monetised YouTube channel, a large Instagram following), [specialist estate planning steps](https://www.hjlaw.com.au/blog/post/12365/the-influencer-estate/) such as testamentary trusts and a tech-competent executor may be needed.*

***

## How to create a digital inventory and appoint a digital executor

A [practical digital legacy plan](https://beconnected.esafety.gov.au/topic-library/articles-and-tips/how-to-prepare-your-digital-legacy-plan) includes four elements: a list of accounts, a nominated digital executor, secure storage for access instructions, and clear wishes for each account.

**What to record for each account:**

- Account name and platform (e.g. Facebook, Gmail, Netflix)
- Username or email address used to log in
- Whether a password is recorded and where (password manager, encrypted file)
- Your wishes: delete, memorialise, or transfer
- Two-factor authentication method and which device holds the authenticator app

**Where to store it securely:**

Store the inventory in a password manager such as 1Password or Bitwarden, or in an encrypted file held by your solicitor. Do not embed passwords in your Will. As noted in Willow Tree Funerals' guide on Wills and funeral decisions, a Will becomes a public document after probate, making any credentials inside it accessible to anyone who requests a copy.

**Appointing a digital executor:**

Choose someone who is tech-literate, discreet, and willing to act promptly. They do not need to be the same person as the legal executor, though coordination between the two is important. Document their role clearly in a letter of wishes kept with the inventory.

**Pro Tip:** *Store the location of your digital inventory (not the inventory itself) in your Will. Your executor then knows where to look without your passwords becoming public record.*

***

## How to preserve photos, videos and messages from a Facebook account

**If you have login access:**

1. Go to Settings & Privacy > Settings > Your Facebook Information > Download Your Information.
2. Select the data types you want (photos, videos, posts, messages) and choose a date range.
3. Request the download. Meta will prepare a file and notify you when it is ready, usually within a few hours to a few days.
4. Save the downloaded archive to at least two locations: an external hard drive and a cloud service such as Google Drive or iCloud.

**If you do not have login access:**

- Request memorialisation first, which preserves the account and its content.
- Ask whether a legacy contact was nominated; that person may be able to request an archive if the account holder pre-authorised it.
- Collect copies from family members' own devices, tagged photos, and shared albums.
- Check the deceased's phone for locally saved photos and back it up before the device is wiped or returned.

**Pro Tip:** *When saving photos for a memorial video or funeral tribute, export original files rather than screenshots. Original files retain timestamps and higher resolution, which matters for printed orders of service and memorial slideshows.*

***

## What to do when you can't access the Facebook account

Not having the password is common. Meta does not provide login credentials to family members, but you can still act.

**Step-by-step request process:**

1. Go to Facebook's Special Request for a Deceased Person's Account.
2. Select whether you are requesting memorialisation or removal.
3. Upload a certified copy of the death certificate and proof of your relationship or executor authority.
4. Submit and note your reference number.

[Lawpath confirms](https://lawpath.com.au/blog/social-media-doesnt-die-so-what-happens-to-your-accounts-when-you-do) that platforms commonly require a death certificate and proof of authority, and that full message access is rarely granted without specific legal orders. Processing times vary but typically range from a few days to several weeks depending on the volume of requests Meta is handling.

**When to seek legal advice:**

- The account holds commercial value (monetised page, business account).
- The estate is contested and account content may be relevant to proceedings.
- A locked email account is blocking access to financial or legal documents.

**Interim measures while you wait:**

- Alert the deceased's bank and superannuation fund.
- Monitor credit activity through a service such as Equifax Australia.
- Notify close contacts that the account is unsecured and to ignore any messages from it.

**Pro Tip:** *If you need a court order to compel platform access, [Australia's regulatory gap](https://www.afterlife.ai/digital-assets-when-you-die-australia/) means this is a specialist area. Seek a solicitor experienced in digital estate law rather than a general practitioner.*

***

## How to protect the family from scams and identity theft after a death

Grief-targeting fraud is a real and growing risk. Scammers monitor obituaries and public social posts to identify recently bereaved families, then impersonate the deceased or pose as funeral-related services.

**Immediate security checklist:**

- Alert all banks and financial institutions and freeze or close accounts as directed.
- Change passwords on any shared email accounts immediately.
- Check all devices for saved login credentials and remove them.
- Set up credit monitoring through Equifax Australia or a similar service.
- Review the deceased's email inbox for subscription services, financial accounts, or active logins that need to be cancelled.

**Common grief-scam tactics to watch for:**

- Messages from the deceased's account asking friends for money or gift cards.
- Fake donation pages using the deceased's name and photo.
- Impersonation calls from people claiming to be the funeral home or a government agency requesting payment.

Report scams to [Scamwatch](https://www.scamwatch.gov.au) (run by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission) and to the platform directly. A brief message to the deceased's friends and family, posted by a trusted family member, warning them that the account may be compromised, is one of the most effective ways to reduce harm quickly.

**Pro Tip:** *Post a single, clear message from a family member's own account stating that the deceased has passed and that any messages from their account should be ignored. This takes two minutes and can prevent significant distress for friends and extended family.*

***

## Managing other social media platforms and online services

Facebook is rarely the only platform that needs attention. Each service has its own process, and [LawConnect's guide](https://lawconnect.com/en-au/guides/social-media-accounts-after-death-australia) confirms that families should prepare a death certificate and proof of relationship for each one.

**Apple:** Apple now offers a Digital Legacy feature, allowing account holders to nominate legacy contacts who can request access to iCloud data (photos, notes, messages) after death. Without a pre-nominated legacy contact and an access key, Apple will not grant family access to the account.

**Google:** Google's Inactive Account Manager lets users nominate trusted contacts and set instructions for their account data. Without this, family members can submit a request through Google's deceased user process, though access to Gmail content is not guaranteed.

**Instagram:** Follows Meta's process. Use the Instagram Special Request form with the same documents required for Facebook.

**LinkedIn:** Offers a form to report a deceased member's profile for removal. Memorialisation is not available; removal is the only option.

**Online banking and subscriptions:** Contact each institution directly with a death certificate and executor papers. Subscriptions (Netflix, Spotify, utilities) should be cancelled promptly to stop ongoing charges to the estate.

***

## How long does Facebook memorialisation or deletion take?

Processing times for Meta requests are not publicly guaranteed and may vary widely depending on circumstances such as document completeness and support queue volume. Memorialisation and deletion requests can take several days to several weeks to process. If a legacy contact was pre-nominated and authorised, they may access and download data shortly after memorialisation.

Delays are more common when documents are incomplete, when the account has been flagged for security review, or when Meta's support queue is high. If you have not received a response within three weeks, resubmit the request with a clear cover note referencing your original submission date.

There is no phone support line for these requests. All contact with Meta on deceased person's accounts is handled through the online forms described below.

***

## How to contact Facebook support for a deceased person's account

Meta does not offer a direct phone line for deceased person's account requests. All requests are handled through online forms.

- **Memorialise an account:** facebook.com/help/contact/234739086860192
- **Request removal of a deceased person's account:** Use the same Special Request form and select the removal option.
- **Instagram requests:** help.instagram.com/264154560391256
- **Meta Help Centre (general):** facebook.com/help

For all requests, have ready: a certified death certificate, your government-issued photo ID, and proof of your relationship to the deceased or your executor authority. Submitting incomplete documents is the most common reason for delays.

***

### A funeral director's perspective on online legacy during arrangements

When a family calls Willow Tree Funerals in those first difficult days, the conversation almost always turns to practical tasks: the death certificate, the service arrangements, and increasingly, what to do about the deceased's social media. Families are often surprised by how much needs to be done online, and how quickly.

At Willow Tree Funerals, Bruce Missen helps families gather the wording for obituary notices and memorial posts, and coordinates the information needed for published death notices. That is practical support the funeral director can genuinely offer. What requires the executor's authority, such as submitting deletion requests or accessing account archives, is a separate matter, and Bruce is clear about that boundary so families do not inadvertently create legal complications.

Willow Tree Funerals serves families across St George, Sutherland Shire, South West Sydney, and the wider Sydney region. Bruce is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and families always speak directly with him. For families who want to include digital legacy instructions in their pre-arrangement, that conversation is part of the planning process.

***

## Willow Tree Funerals: practical support for memorial notices and online legacy

When you are arranging a funeral, the last thing you need is to navigate Meta's help pages alone. Willow Tree Funerals provides direct, personal support for families across Sydney, including assistance with funeral notice wording, memorial video tributes, and the practical details that make a public tribute meaningful.

[![Willow Tree Funerals](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1780021199999_willowtreefunerals.jpg)](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/)

Bruce Missen personally handles every arrangement and is available around the clock. Willow Tree Funerals can assist with writing obituary and death notice copy, preparing memorial video tributes (from $375), and advising on appropriate wording for social media posts. For families who want to record their own digital legacy wishes as part of a [pre-arranged funeral plan](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/pre-arrange), that is part of the conversation from the start.

To speak with Bruce directly, call **02 8776 1667** or visit [Willowtreefunerals](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au). Families in [North Sydney](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/funeral-director-north-sydney), Penrith, and across greater Sydney are welcome to reach out at any hour.

***

## Sources

Official resources for Australian families managing a deceased person's online accounts:

- [What happens to your digital accounts after you die | eSafety Commissioner](https://www.esafety.gov.au/key-topics/digital-wellbeing/what-happens-to-your-digital-accounts-after-you-die/)

- [The influencer estate — HJLaw (blog)](https://www.hjlaw.com.au/blog/post/12365/the-influencer-estate/)

***

This article is general information, not a substitute for advice from a qualified lawyer. Consult a qualified legal professional about your own circumstances before acting on anything here.

## FAQ

### What happens to a Facebook account when someone dies?

Facebook keeps the account active until a family member or executor submits a request. You can ask Meta to memorialise the account (adding "Remembering" to the profile) or permanently delete it using the Special Request form.

### Can an executor log into a deceased person's Facebook account in Australia?

Generally no. Australian law does not grant executors the right to log into platform accounts, and Meta will not provide login credentials. Executors can request memorialisation or deletion by submitting a death certificate and proof of authority.

### How long does Facebook memorialisation take?

Requests submitted with complete documents are typically processed within a few days to two weeks. Incomplete submissions are the most common cause of delays.

### What is a Facebook legacy contact?

A legacy contact is a person the account holder nominates in advance to manage their memorialised profile. They can pin a tribute post and, if pre-authorised, download an archive of the account's data, but they cannot log in or read private messages.

### Who can help with obituary wording and memorial notices in Sydney?

Willow Tree Funerals, based in Hurstville and Macquarie Links, assists families across Sydney with obituary copy, death notice wording, and memorial video tributes. Bruce Missen is available 24/7 on 02 8776 1667.

title: Residuary estate in a will: what you need to know
excerpt: Discover the definition of residuary estate and learn how to ensure your assets are allocated according to your wishes in your will.
content:
![Will and urn on desk with white lily](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1786202043726_Will-and-urn-on-desk-with-white-lily.jpeg)

The **residuary estate** is the portion of a deceased person's estate that remains after all debts, funeral expenses, administration costs, taxes, and specific gifts named in the will have been settled. In plain terms, it is everything left over once the estate's obligations are met. Under Australian law, this definition is [well established](https://www.cairnswillsandestates.com.au/blog/understanding-legal-terms-residuary-estate-in-a-will/): the residue acts as a catch-all for assets not individually itemised in the will, including property acquired after the will was signed. If you are making a will, the single most important step you can take is to name at least one residuary beneficiary and at least one alternate. Failing to do so risks partial intestacy, where state law rather than your wishes determines who receives what.

***

## Key takeaways

The residuary estate is the legal foundation of any well-drafted will: name a residuary beneficiary and at least one alternate, or state intestacy rules will decide what happens to everything not covered by a specific gift.

| Point | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Define the residue clearly | The residuary estate covers all assets remaining after debts, funeral costs, taxes, and specific gifts are settled. |
| Name a beneficiary and alternate | Without both, partial intestacy applies and state law distributes the residue, which may not reflect your wishes. |
| Check what bypasses the estate | Superannuation with binding nominations, joint tenancy property, and life policies with named beneficiaries do not form part of the residue. |
| Executors: follow the statutory order | Pay funeral costs first, then administration expenses, debts, and taxes, before calculating and distributing the residue. |
| Seek legal advice for complexity | Blended families, business interests, and overseas assets require specialist drafting beyond a standard will kit. |

***

## Table of Contents

- [What does the residuary estate actually include?](#what-does-the-residuary-estate-actually-include)
- [Why every will should include a residuary clause](#why-every-will-should-include-a-residuary-clause)
- [How to draft a residuary clause and nominate beneficiaries](#how-to-draft-a-residuary-clause-and-nominate-beneficiaries)
- [Sample residuary clauses you can discuss with your lawyer](#sample-residuary-clauses-you-can-discuss-with-your-lawyer)
- [What happens if you don't name a residuary beneficiary?](#what-happens-if-you-dont-name-a-residuary-beneficiary)
- [Who can inherit the residuary estate?](#who-can-inherit-the-residuary-estate)
- [Executor's checklist for administering the residuary estate](#executors-checklist-for-administering-the-residuary-estate)
- [Practical tips for executors and beneficiaries](#practical-tips-for-executors-and-beneficiaries)
- [A note from Willow Tree Funerals](#a-note-from-willow-tree-funerals)
- [How Willow Tree Funerals can help your family](#how-willow-tree-funerals-can-help-your-family)
- [Sources](#sources)
- [FAQ](#faq)

## What does the residuary estate actually include?

Before the residue can be calculated, the estate must meet its obligations in a prescribed order. Australian estate law sets out that funeral expenses are paid first, followed by administration costs, then tax liabilities and other debts. Only after those are cleared does the residue take shape.

What typically forms the residuary estate:

- Unspecified personal property (furniture, jewellery, vehicles not named in a specific gift)
- Real estate not individually gifted to a named beneficiary
- The cash balance remaining after specific monetary gifts are paid
- Investments, shares, and savings accounts not otherwise disposed of
- Assets acquired after the will was made, provided no other instrument disposes of them

A simple example makes the distinction clear. Suppose a will says: "I give my home at 14 Smith Street to my daughter Anna." That is a specific gift. The clause "I give the residue of my estate to my son James" then captures everything else, including a term deposit opened two years after the will was signed. Anna gets the house; James gets the rest.

One category of assets commonly causes confusion. Jointly held property passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant by right of survivorship, bypassing the estate entirely. Similarly, life insurance policies with a binding beneficiary nomination and [superannuation death benefits](https://www.simplyestate.com.au/deceased-estate/assets-residuary-estate/) with a valid binding nomination do not form part of the estate and therefore cannot be part of the residue. Executors who overlook this distinction risk miscalculating the residue and creating disputes.

The residuary estate is [not merely leftover cash](https://www.mondaq.com/australia/wills-intestacy-estate-planning/1417280/what-does-residuary-estate-mean-in-a-will). It can include real estate, investment portfolios, and personal effects of significant value. Its size does not change the need for a clear residuary clause.

***

## Why every will should include a residuary clause

A residuary clause prevents partial intestacy. That is the short answer, and it is reason enough on its own.

When a will omits a residuary beneficiary, any assets not covered by specific gifts fall outside the will's reach. Those assets are then distributed under the intestacy rules of the relevant state or territory, which may bear no resemblance to the deceased's actual wishes. In the worst case, where no eligible next-of-kin can be identified, the residue may be declared *bona vacantia* and pass to the Crown.

A well-drafted residuary clause also keeps the will concise. Rather than listing every possible asset, the will-maker can name specific gifts for particular items and direct everything else to the residuary beneficiary. This approach automatically captures assets acquired after the will is signed, without requiring the will to be updated every time circumstances change. It also allows different treatment for named gifts and the remainder: a family heirloom to one child, the financial residue shared equally among all children.

Disputes over estates frequently arise not from contested specific gifts but from ambiguity about what falls into the residue. A clear clause reduces that ambiguity. State intestacy rules differ across jurisdictions, so if you are unsure how your state's rules would apply, checking the relevant legislation on [AustLII](http://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/qld/consol_act/sa1981138/sch2.html) or seeking legal advice is the prudent step.

***

## How to draft a residuary clause and nominate beneficiaries

Name a primary residuary beneficiary and at least one substitute. That is the starting point for any residuary clause. If the primary beneficiary predeceases you and no alternate is named, the gift lapses and the asset falls into partial intestacy.

A practical drafting checklist:

1. Identify who receives the residue: a spouse, children, a charity, a trust, or a combination.
2. Decide whether the residue is shared and, if so, in what proportions (equal shares or specific percentages).
3. Name at least one alternate beneficiary in case the primary beneficiary does not survive you.
4. If leaving a share to a charity, use its full legal name and ABN to avoid ambiguity.
5. Consider a residuary trust if beneficiaries include minors or if staged distribution is preferred.
6. Use the phrase "the residue of my estate" consistently throughout the will to avoid drafting conflicts.
7. Review the clause whenever you acquire significant new assets or your family circumstances change.

Three common clause structures suit different situations. A **single beneficiary clause** directs the entire residue to one person, with one named alternate. A **shared residue clause** splits the residue among two or more beneficiaries by percentage or equal shares, with alternates for each. A **residuary trust clause** holds the residue on trust, often for children until they reach a specified age, managed by a trustee.

**Pro Tip:** *Avoid describing a beneficiary by role alone ("my eldest child") rather than by name. If family circumstances change, role-based descriptions can create ambiguity. Always use full legal names and consider adding a date of birth for clarity.*

Legal advice is worth seeking when the estate includes business interests, overseas assets, a blended family, or a beneficiary with a disability. These situations often require specialist drafting that a standard will kit cannot reliably address. Naming alternates and specifying shares are the two most consistent pieces of advice from estate lawyers across Australia.

***

## Sample residuary clauses you can discuss with your lawyer

Choose the example that best matches your intention, then discuss it with a solicitor before finalising your will. These samples use plain Australian wording and are intended as starting points, not final legal text.

**Single beneficiary with alternate:**

*Suitable for: a straightforward estate where one person inherits everything. Check whether a thirty-day survivorship clause suits your circumstances.*

**Two beneficiaries with percentages:**

*Suitable for: unequal distribution between two beneficiaries. Confirm the percentages add to [100%](https://scholarship.law.marquette.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=5335\&context=mulr) and that the alternate arrangements reflect your wishes.*

**Residuary trust for minor beneficiaries:**

*Suitable for: estates where beneficiaries are minors or where staged distribution is preferred. A solicitor should confirm the trustee powers are adequate and that the trust complies with your state's legislation.*

**Residue to a charity:**

*Suitable for: charitable bequests. Always use the charity's full legal name and ABN, and name an alternate in case the charity no longer operates.*

***

## What happens if you don't name a residuary beneficiary?

Omitting a residuary beneficiary does not leave assets in limbo indefinitely. It triggers partial intestacy, meaning the unallocated portion of the estate is distributed according to the intestacy rules of the deceased's state or territory, regardless of what the rest of the will says.

Those rules follow a statutory formula that prioritises surviving spouses and children, then more distant relatives. If no eligible next-of-kin can be found, the residue may be declared *bona vacantia* and pass to the Crown. The outcome may bear no resemblance to what the deceased intended.

The Queensland intestacy schedule, available on AustLII, provides a concrete illustration of how residue can be allocated under intestacy rules. The table below uses that schedule as an example only. Rules differ by state and territory, so always check the legislation for your jurisdiction.

| Surviving relatives (Queensland example) | How the residuary estate is distributed |
| --- | --- |
| Spouse only, no children | Spouse receives the entire residuary estate |
| Spouse and children of that relationship | Spouse receives household chattels and a statutory fraction of the remaining residue; children share the balance |
| Children only, no spouse | Children share the residuary estate equally |
| No spouse, no children | Parents, then siblings, then more distant relatives in statutory order |
| No eligible next-of-kin | Residue may become *bona vacantia* and pass to the Crown |

*Source: Schedule 2, Succession Act 1981 (Qld) via AustLII. This is an illustrative example. Confirm the rules for your state or territory before relying on them.*

***

## Who can inherit the residuary estate?

Residuary beneficiaries can be individuals, charities, corporate trustees, or a combination. The law does not restrict who may be named, though some categories carry practical considerations.

Common beneficiary types include:

- A spouse or de facto partner
- Children (including adult children and stepchildren, depending on the will's wording)
- Other family members or close friends
- Registered charities (identified by full legal name and ABN)
- Corporate trustees holding the residue on trust for beneficiaries

A gift to a residuary beneficiary lapses if that person predeceases the testator and no alternate is named. Some jurisdictions have anti-lapse provisions that may redirect a lapsed gift to the deceased beneficiary's children, but these provisions vary and cannot be relied upon as a substitute for naming alternates explicitly.

Certain assets bypass the residue entirely regardless of who is named. Superannuation with a binding death benefit nomination, life insurance with a named beneficiary, and property held as joint tenants all pass outside the estate. A will-maker who intends to benefit a particular person from those assets needs to update the relevant nominations directly, not through the will's residuary clause.

***

## Executor's checklist for administering the residuary estate

The executor's job is to collect the estate's assets, pay its obligations in the correct order, and then distribute what remains to the residuary beneficiaries as the will directs. [Legal Aid Victoria](https://www.legalaid.vic.gov.au/administration-estate) confirms that a grant of probate or letters of administration is required before dealing with most estate assets, unless the estate qualifies as small under the relevant court's threshold.

A practical step-by-step checklist:

1. **Locate the will** and confirm you are the named executor.
2. **Apply for a grant of probate** (or letters of administration if there is no will) from the Supreme Court of your state or territory, unless the estate qualifies as small.
3. **Map all assets**, noting which bypass the estate (joint tenancy property, superannuation with binding nominations, life policies with named beneficiaries).
4. **Value the estate assets** as at the date of death.
5. **Pay funeral and administration costs** first, keeping all receipts. Funeral expenses are typically the first liability settled from the estate.
6. **Settle all debts and tax liabilities**, including any outstanding income tax and, where applicable, estate duties.
7. **Distribute specific gifts** named in the will to the relevant beneficiaries.
8. **Calculate the residue** from what remains after steps 5–7.
9. **Distribute the residue** to the residuary beneficiaries in the proportions the will specifies.
10. **Prepare final estate accounts** and make them available to residuary beneficiaries, who are entitled to inspect them.
11. **Finalise the estate**, including closing accounts and lodging any required returns.

Simple estates can often be finalised within 6–12 months. Complex estates or contested distributions commonly take well over 12 months. Poor record-keeping is one of the most common causes of delay and can expose an executor to personal liability.

***

## Practical tips for executors and beneficiaries

Clear preparation before death and careful administration after it are what prevent most residuary estate disputes. A few high-value actions make a significant difference.

- **Name alternates in the will.** If the primary residuary beneficiary predeceases the testator, an alternate prevents partial intestacy.
- **Keep the will current.** Review it after major life events: marriage, divorce, the birth of children, or the acquisition of significant new assets.
- **Document specific gifts separately.** A letter of wishes accompanying the will can clarify the testator's intentions without creating legally binding obligations that complicate the residue.
- **Check superannuation and life insurance nominations.** These pass outside the estate. An outdated nomination can direct assets to an unintended recipient regardless of what the will says.
- **Executors: communicate early and often.** Transparent communication with residuary beneficiaries reduces disputes and protects the executor from claims of mismanagement.

**Pro Tip:** *Funeral costs are among the first liabilities paid from the estate. Keeping the funeral invoice, receipts for disbursements, and a record of any pre-arranged funeral contract makes the executor's accounting straightforward and reduces the risk of disputes. A guide to funeral disbursements explains exactly what receipts to retain.*

Seek formal legal advice when the estate includes business interests, overseas assets, a beneficiary with a disability, or a blended family. These situations carry risks that standard will kits and general guidance cannot adequately address. For executors managing estates with overseas elements, a [post-funeral administration checklist](https://blog.indianlifememorial.com/blog/post-funeral-admin-tasks-checklist) can help map the additional steps involved.

***

## A note from Willow Tree Funerals

A clear residuary clause in a well-prepared will prevents the majority of post-death estate problems we see families navigate during an already difficult time.

At Willow Tree Funerals, we regularly work with families who are administering estates while simultaneously managing grief and funeral arrangements. Laws governing residuary estates and intestacy differ across Australian states and territories. The sources below are the most reliable starting points for verifying details in your jurisdiction.

- [Understanding Legal Terms: Residuary Estate In A Will | Cairns Wills & Estate Lawyers](https://www.cairnswillsandestates.com.au/blog/understanding-legal-terms-residuary-estate-in-a-will/)

AustLII is the central resource for checking the legislation in your state or territory. Laws differ, and a provision that applies in Queensland may not apply in the same way in New South Wales or Victoria.

***

This article is general information, not a substitute for advice from a qualified lawyer. Consult a qualified legal professional about your own circumstances before acting on anything here.

## FAQ

### What is the meaning of residuary estate?

The residuary estate is everything that remains in a deceased person's estate after all debts, funeral expenses, administration costs, taxes, and specific gifts named in the will have been paid. It acts as a catch-all for assets not individually listed in the will, including property acquired after the will was signed.

### What is a residuary estate in Australia?

In Australia, the residuary estate is the portion of a deceased's estate distributed to the residuary beneficiary named in the will, once all obligations and specific bequests are settled. If no residuary beneficiary is named, the residue passes under the intestacy rules of the relevant state or territory.

### Who is entitled to the residuary estate?

The person or persons named as residuary beneficiaries in the will are entitled to the residue. If no residuary beneficiary is named, or if the named beneficiary has predeceased the testator and no alternate is specified, the residue is distributed under state intestacy rules, which prioritise spouses, children, and then more distant relatives.

### What is an example of a residuary estate?

If a will leaves a specific house to one child and a gift to a charity, the residuary estate is everything else: the remaining cash, investments, personal property, and any assets acquired after the will was made. A residuary clause such as "I give the residue of my estate to my spouse" directs all of that remainder to the named person.

title: Free will kit online: legally valid options for Australians
excerpt: Discover legally valid free will kits online for Australians. Create your will easily with trusted options for all budgets and needs.
content:
![Signing a Will with two witnesses present](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1786314513073_Signing-a-Will-with-two-witnesses-present.jpeg)

Yes, you can use a free will kit online in Australia. The document you draft becomes legally binding once it is printed and executed correctly under your state's formalities. The key requirement is straightforward: the Will must be in writing, signed by you, and witnessed by two adults who are not beneficiaries. That rule holds whether you drafted the document on a platform costing nothing or paid a solicitor.

The most commonly used free and low-cost options for Australians are:

- **EveryWill** — free drafting and lifetime updates via charity partnerships (Heart Foundation, Fred Hollows Foundation)
- **Safewill** — discounted paid option with optional solicitor review, also available free through select charity partners
- **Willed** — paid service with faster completion and optional review support
- **Bare** (bare.com.au) — guided step-through platform for Australian users
- **Australia Post Will Kit** — downloadable, printable template for offline completion
- **Willow Tree Funerals** — in-person pre-arrangement assistance for families who prefer face-to-face support in Sydney

One execution rule overrides everything else: plan your two independent adult witnesses before you print. Remote or audio-visual link (AVL) witnessing is permitted in some states under the [Electronic Transactions Act](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/nsw/consol_act/eta2000256/s14g.html), but the rules differ by jurisdiction and must be confirmed for your state before you rely on them.

***

## Key takeaways

A free online will kit is legally valid in Australia provided the finished document is printed, signed by the will-maker, and witnessed by two independent adults in accordance with your state's formalities.

| Point | Details |
|---|---|
| Execution is what matters | Drafting online is fine; validity depends on correct signing and witnessing after you print. |
| Choose the right kit | EveryWill is free via charity partners; Safewill and Willed offer paid options with optional solicitor review. |
| AVL witnessing is state-specific | Remote witnessing under the Electronic Transactions Act is permitted in NSW but rules differ across states. |
| Re-execute after every change | Download a fresh copy, re-print, and re-witness — never annotate an existing signed Will. |
| Willow Tree Funerals | Offers in-person pre-arrangement support and solicitor referrals for Sydney families who need help beyond a DIY kit. |

***

## Table of Contents

- [Which free online will kit suits you? A side-by-side comparison](#which-free-online-will-kit-suits-you-a-side-by-side-comparison)
- [Who should use a free online will kit — and who should not](#who-should-use-a-free-online-will-kit-and-who-should-not)
- [How to make a Will online: fields to prepare and steps to follow](#how-to-make-a-will-online-fields-to-prepare-and-steps-to-follow)
- [How to make an online-drafted Will legally valid in Australia](#how-to-make-an-online-drafted-will-legally-valid-in-australia)
- [Common pitfalls with online Wills and when to see a lawyer](#common-pitfalls-with-online-wills-and-when-to-see-a-lawyer)
- [A funeral director's perspective on Wills and what families actually face](#a-funeral-directors-perspective-on-wills-and-what-families-actually-face)
- [Pre-arrangement support from Willow Tree Funerals](#pre-arrangement-support-from-willow-tree-funerals)
- [Sources](#sources)
- [FAQ](#faq)

## Which free online will kit suits you? A side-by-side comparison

"Free" refers to drafting cost only. Printing, professional witnessing, and any solicitor review may carry small additional costs.

![Comparison diagram of free will kits features in Australia](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1786314893785_Comparison-diagram-of-free-will-kits-features-in-Australia.jpeg)

As the [Fred Hollows Foundation notes](https://www.hollows.org/gift-in-your-will/online-wills/), charity-partnered platforms such as EveryWill, Safewill, and Willed produce a downloadable Will that becomes legally binding once printed and signed correctly. The [Heart Foundation confirms](https://www.heartfoundation.org.au/gifts-in-wills/online-wills) that many platforms support updates by re-execution, meaning you download a fresh copy and re-sign after any changes.

***

## Who should use a free online will kit — and who should not

A free or low-cost digital will kit suits most straightforward situations. If your circumstances are simple, there is no reason to pay solicitor rates for a basic document.

**A free kit is generally appropriate when you:**

- Have a straightforward estate (a home, savings, superannuation, personal property)
- Want to leave everything to one or two beneficiaries with no conditions
- Need to appoint a guardian for minor children with no contested family arrangements
- Are updating an existing Will after a minor life change (new address, updated executor)

**Seek a solicitor when any of the following apply:**

- You hold assets in more than one country
- Your estate includes a business, trust, or complex investment structure
- There is a blended family or a prior relationship with potential competing claims
- A beneficiary has a disability requiring a special disability trust
- You have reason to believe the Will may be contested
- You are in hospital or aged care and capacity may be questioned

Some law firms can attend hospitals or aged-care facilities to draft and execute a Will in urgent situations, and video-call drafting services also exist for time-critical cases, as Falzon Legal notes.

**Pro Tip:** *Confirm your two witnesses are available and independent before you open any online platform. Execution is the most common failure point for online Wills — not the drafting itself.*

***

## How to make a Will online: fields to prepare and steps to follow

Most Australian online Will platforms walk you through the same core questions. Gathering this information before you start means you can complete a kit in a single sitting.

**Documents and details to have ready:**

- Full legal name, date of birth, and residential address
- Asset list: property titles, bank accounts, superannuation fund details, vehicle registrations, investment accounts
- Beneficiary full names, relationships, and contact details
- Executor full name and contact details (plus an alternate executor)
- Guardian names for any minor children
- Specific gift details (who receives what item or sum)

### The typical step-by-step fields

1. **Personal details and capacity confirmation** — your full legal name, address, date of birth, and a declaration that you are making the Will freely and of sound mind.
2. **Asset inventory** — list property, financial accounts, superannuation, vehicles, and personal items of value.
3. **Beneficiaries** — name each person and their relationship to you; specify shares or specific items.
4. **Specific gifts and pecuniary legacies** — individual items or fixed cash amounts to named people or organisations.
5. **Residuary estate** — who receives everything not covered by specific gifts, and in what proportions.
6. **Executor appointment** — the person responsible for administering your estate; name an alternate in case the primary executor cannot act.
7. **Executor powers** — most platforms include standard powers; read these carefully before accepting defaults.
8. **Guardians for minor children** — name a guardian and an alternate; include any relevant wishes about upbringing.
9. **Funeral wishes and organ donation** — these are not legally binding directions, but they guide your executor and family.
10. **Alternate beneficiaries** — what happens if a primary beneficiary dies before you.
11. **Signature and witness instructions** — the platform will generate a completed PDF with signing instructions; follow them precisely.

Treat any update as a fresh execution event. Download a new copy, re-print, and re-witness rather than annotating an existing document. The Heart Foundation's guidance on online Wills is consistent on this point: re-execution is the correct process after every substantive change.

***

## How to make an online-drafted Will legally valid in Australia

Drafting online is the easy part. Validity depends entirely on what happens after you click "download."

### Core execution requirements

[NSW Government guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/family-and-relationships/planning-for-end-of-life/learn-about-wills) sets out the standard formalities that apply across Australian states: the Will must be in writing, signed by the will-maker, and witnessed by two adults who are not beneficiaries. Witnesses must sign in the testator's presence and record the date. These requirements are not optional and cannot be waived by a platform's terms of service.

1. **Print** the completed Will document in full.
2. **Sign** every page where indicated, in the presence of both witnesses simultaneously.
3. **Witnesses sign** in your presence, on the same occasion, and record the date.
4. **Witnesses must not be beneficiaries** — or the spouse or de facto partner of a beneficiary — or their gift may be voided.
5. **Date the Will** clearly on the execution page.

### Remote and audio-visual witnessing

Section 14G of the Electronic Transactions Act permits witnessing by audio-visual link in NSW, provided the witness can observe the signing in real time, signs a counterpart of the document, and endorses it with a note of the method used. Victoria introduced its own remote execution procedure under amendments to the Wills Act 1997, with [section 8A](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/vic/consol_act/wa199791/s8a.html) setting out specific requirements. Other states have varying provisions, and AVL witnessing is a jurisdictional compliance question — do not assume the NSW or Victorian rules apply in Queensland, South Australia, or Western Australia without checking your state's current legislation.

The Law Society's guidance on electronic witnessing recommends that the attestation clause record the method used and that witnesses confirm they could see the testator and the signing action in real time. If you use AVL witnessing, record this on the document itself.

> **A critical point:** AVL provisions allow remote witnessing of a physical signature. They do not permit electronic signatures as a substitute for a wet-ink signature on a printed Will. The document must still be printed and physically signed.

State Trustees confirm that the format of drafting — online or otherwise — does not change the validity fundamentals. The primary risk is failing to meet witnessing requirements, not using an online platform.

***

## Common pitfalls with online Wills and when to see a lawyer

Most online Will failures are avoidable. They cluster around a handful of predictable errors.

**Common pitfalls to avoid:**

- Witnesses who are beneficiaries (or their spouses/partners) — this can void the gift to that person
- Witnesses signing at different times or not in the testator's presence
- Handwritten amendments to a printed Will without re-execution
- Failing to re-execute after a major life event (marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary)
- Vague guardianship wording that leaves room for dispute
- Appointing an executor who lives overseas or is unlikely to be available

**Red flags that mean you should see a solicitor:**

- Any asset held outside Australia
- A business interest, partnership, or trust
- A family situation involving children from prior relationships
- A beneficiary with a disability or dependency
- Any reason to expect a challenge to the Will's validity
- Doubt about your own capacity at the time of signing

Before paying full solicitor rates, consider the middle ground. Charity partner programmes through EveryWill, Safewill, and Willed frequently offer free or subsidised drafting plus an optional paid solicitor review, which is a practical option for estates that are mostly straightforward but carry one or two complications. Estate planning resources through partners such as [Indian Life Memorial's will and estate services](https://indianlifememorial.com/services/will-estate) can also provide useful orientation before you engage a solicitor directly.

***

## A funeral director's perspective on Wills and what families actually face

There is a detail that online Will guides rarely mention: the Will is often the last document a family can find when they need it most.

![Urn and secure storage for Will documents](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1786314504518_Urn-and-secure-storage-for-Will-documents.jpeg)

In my experience at Willow Tree Funerals, the families who navigate bereavement with the least distress are those where the will-maker told their executor exactly where the original Will was stored — and where the funeral wishes were recorded separately, in a place accessible before probate is granted. A Will held by a solicitor or in a safe-deposit box is legally sound. However, if the executor cannot locate it within days of a death, it creates real practical difficulty at an already painful time.

The interaction between a Will and funeral arrangements matters more than most people realise. Funeral decisions are typically made within 24–48 hours of a death, often before a Will has been located or read. Recording funeral wishes in a separate, accessible document — and telling your executor and family where it is — removes a significant burden from the people you love. The Will itself can then do its proper work through the probate process without being pressed into service as an emergency instruction sheet.

For families who want guidance beyond a digital kit, Willow Tree Funerals offers [pre-arrangement services](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/pre-arrange) that include help with documenting wishes, understanding what executors need, and connecting families with local solicitors where required.

***

## Pre-arrangement support from Willow Tree Funerals

Online Will kits handle the drafting. What they cannot do is sit with you, answer your specific questions, or help you think through the practical steps that follow.

[![Willow Tree Funerals](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1780021199999_willowtreefunerals.jpg)](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/)

Willow Tree Funerals offers pre-arranged funeral planning for families across Sydney, Wollongong, and the Central Coast. Bruce Missen works directly with families to document funeral wishes, explain what executors will need, and refer clients to local solicitors or witnesses where an online kit is not sufficient. Prices are published openly, funds are held in a regulated trust, and today's prices are locked in at the time of arrangement. For families in the North Shore, Inner West, or South West Sydney who prefer a conversation over a web form, call 02 8776 1667 or visit the pre-arrangement page to begin.

***

**Online Will platforms:**

If you live outside NSW or Victoria, check your state government's current Succession Act and any COVID-era amendments that may still be in force. Remote witnessing rules introduced as temporary measures have been made permanent in some jurisdictions and remain temporary or lapsed in others.

***

This article is general information, not a substitute for advice from a qualified lawyer. Consult a qualified legal professional about your own circumstances before acting on anything here.

## FAQ

### Are free will kits legal in Australia?

Yes. A Will drafted using a free online kit or downloadable template is legally valid in Australia provided it is printed, signed by the will-maker, and witnessed by two adults who are not beneficiaries, in accordance with your state's Succession Act requirements.

### Is the Australia Post Will Kit legal?

The Australia Post Will Kit is a printable template that produces a valid Will when completed and executed correctly. Validity depends on following the witnessing and signing formalities for your state, not on where the template came from.

### Are online Wills legal in Australia?

Yes. State Trustees confirm that online drafting does not affect validity. The document must still be printed and executed with two independent adult witnesses present.

### What is the best online will kit in Australia?

For a free option, EveryWill is widely used through charity partnerships and offers lifetime updates. Safewill suits those wanting an optional solicitor review at low cost. For families in Sydney who prefer in-person guidance, Willow Tree Funerals offers pre-arrangement support and can refer you to local solicitors.

The one confirmed public record for Jill Irish is the [funeral notice published in The Sydney Morning Herald Tributes](https://tributes.smh.com.au/au/obituaries/smh-au/name/jill-irish-obituary?id=60101613): **Jill Frances IRISH**, born 3 March 1944, passed away 13 November 2025. Her funeral was held at 1pm on Friday 21 November 2025 at 12 Apostles Catholic Church, Jindalee. The notice requests donations to the QAGOMA Foundation's Art & Dementia Program.

Three details to confirm you have the right person at a glance:

- **Full name variant:** Jill Frances IRISH (surname in capitals, as printed in the notice)
- **Birth and death years:** 1944–2025
- **Service:** 1pm, Friday 21 November 2025, 12 Apostles Catholic Church, Jindalee

***

## Key takeaways

The single most important action after finding the Jill Irish SMH Tributes notice is to verify the three core details — full name, dates, and the Jindalee service — before taking any further steps.

| Point | Details |

| Primary source | The SMH Tributes notice is the authoritative record for Jill Frances Irish (1944–2025). |
| Verification shortcut | The nickname Jillypops in the notice is the fastest way to confirm the correct obituary. |
| Donation pathway | Call Alana Acton on 07 3840 7316 to donate to the QAGOMA Foundation's Art & Dementia Program. |
| Social search caution | More than 20 LinkedIn profiles share the name; use Frances, Jindalee, and 1944 to disambiguate. |
| Local funeral support | Willow Tree Funerals offers 24/7 direct access to a funeral director for families in Sydney. |

## How to verify the Jill Irish obituary notice

When a name is as common as Jill Irish, confirming you have the right record matters. Follow these steps in order.

1. **Check the SMH Tributes entry directly.** The [published notice](https://tributes.smh.com.au/au/obituaries/smh-au/name/jill-irish-obituary?id=60101613) is the primary record. Confirm the full name variant (Jill Frances IRISH), birth date (3 March 1944) and death date (13 November 2025) match what you already know.
2. **Cross-reference dates and family names.** The notice lists relatives and uses the nickname Jillypops. If those details align with what family members have told you, you have the right person.
3. **Search surname obituary aggregators.** [Legacy's Irish family obituary index](https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/name/irish) lists many notices under the Irish surname and allows you to set alerts for new entries. Use it to rule out other recent notices for people with the same name.
4. **Contact the funeral director listed in the notice.** The funeral director is the correct first point of contact for service attendance, floral tributes, and any corrections to the published notice.
5. **Check cemetery or service records.** For the Jindalee service, the 12 Apostles Catholic Church parish office can confirm service details if you need written verification.

**Pro Tip:** *The nickname Jillypops, printed in the SMH notice, is the fastest disambiguation tool. If a family member recognises that name immediately, you have confirmed the right obituary without needing any other document.*

***

## Donation instructions from the notice and how to follow them

The published notice requests donations to the **QAGOMA Foundation: Art & Dementia Program**, with Alana Acton named as the contact on **07 3840 7316**.

![Tealight candle and white flowers on table](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1786349373270_Tealight-candle-and-white-flowers-on-table.jpeg)

| 2. Request a receipt | Ask for a tax-deductible receipt at the time of donating; the QAGOMA Foundation is a registered Australian cultural institution |
| 3. Reference the deceased | Quote "In memory of Jill Frances Irish" when making the donation so it is recorded against her tribute |
| 4. Keep your records | Retain the receipt and note the date; families sometimes compile a list of donations received for their own tribute records |

**Pro Tip:** *Always phone the named contact before transferring funds. Donation channels occasionally change after a notice is published, and a brief call protects both your money and the family's tribute record.*

## How to search for social profiles linked to Jill Irish

The name Jill Irish is shared by many people. LinkedIn's directory lists more than 20 profiles under that name, and [Facebook's public listings](https://www.facebook.com/public/Jill-Irish/) show multiple entries as well. Disambiguation is necessary before reaching out to anyone.

Practical search tips:

- Add the middle name Frances or the initial F to any search query.
- Include "Jindalee" or "Brisbane" as a location filter, since the service was held at a Brisbane church.
- Search alongside relatives' names if you know them from the notice.
- Use birth year ranges (1944) to filter results on people-search directories.

Do and don't guidance for contacting profiles you find:

- **Do** send a brief, respectful private message if you believe you have located a relative.
- **Do** state clearly who you are and why you are reaching out.
- **Don't** post publicly on a profile page about the death before confirming the person is aware.
- **Don't** assume any social profile belongs to the deceased; the name is common and the person listed may be entirely unrelated.

If you are next of kin or a close friend who has just seen the notice, your first call should be to the funeral director listed in the published SMH Tributes entry. Have the following ready: the deceased's full name and date of death, your relationship to her, and any specific questions about attendance or floral tributes.

Common administrative tasks families need help with after a notice is published include confirming service attendance numbers, arranging flowers through the funeral home, handling donation enquiries directed to the family, and requesting corrections to the published notice if any detail is wrong.

## How to send condolences and make a donation in Jill's name

Sending condolences well is a small act of care that means a great deal to a grieving family.

1. **Write a condolence card.** Address it to the immediate family by name if you know them. A simple, sincere line is enough: *"Thinking of you and your family with great love and sympathy."* For guidance on addressing the envelope correctly, Willow Tree Funerals has published [practical advice on sympathy cards](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/blog/how-to-address-a-sympathy-card).
2. **Attend the service.** The 12 Apostles Catholic Church, Jindalee service was held at 1pm on Friday 21 November 2025. If you missed it, a note to the family explaining you were thinking of them is always welcome.
3. **Make a donation in her name.** Call Alana Acton on 07 3840 7316 and say: *"I would like to make a donation in memory of Jill Frances Irish."* This ensures the gift is recorded correctly against her tribute.
4. **Send a donation note to the family.** A brief card saying *"A donation has been made to the QAGOMA Foundation's Art & Dementia Program in Jill's memory"* lets the family know their loved one is being honoured.

Do not send flowers to the family home without checking first. Do not post condolences on social media before confirming the family has made a public announcement.

***

## A note from the funeral director

Families who find a published notice and are unsure what to do next often carry more uncertainty than they need to. The notice itself tells you almost everything: who to call, where to go, and where to direct donations.

What it cannot always tell you is how to navigate the hours and days that follow, particularly when relatives are scattered across different states or when the administrative tasks feel unfamiliar. That is where a local funeral director makes a practical difference.
