- [FAQ](#faq)

## What an open casket viewing involves and what to expect

An open casket viewing allows family and friends to see the deceased before burial or cremation, usually in a chapel, church, or funeral home viewing room. The body is prepared beforehand, often with embalming, dressing in chosen clothing, and the placement of personal items such as rosary beads, photographs, or a favourite object. This preparation shapes how the family experiences the moment: careful presentation can offer real comfort, while a rushed or unclear process can add distress at an already painful time.

Viewings can take several forms depending on what the family needs.

- A short visitation before the service, often an hour or two.
- An extended viewing over a day or more, common in some cultural and religious traditions.
- Private family time, arranged separately from the public visitation.

A good funeral director will walk you through what the body will look like, discuss options such as [embalming](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/blog/embalming-in-australia) honestly, and never assume a family wants full disclosure of every detail before they are ready to hear it.

## Why some families choose an open casket

Viewing the body helps many people accept that a death has genuinely happened, which can be a meaningful part of processing grief. [Qualitative research into family experiences of viewing](https://opus.lib.uts.edu.au/bitstream/10453/148325/2/IJPN-S-21-00042%20%281%29%20%281%29%20Submitted.pdf) found that viewing supports memory making and grieving for many mourners, though responses vary widely from person to person.

Common reasons families choose to view include:

- A need for closure, especially after a sudden or unexpected death.
- The chance to form a final memory and say a proper goodbye.
- Religious or cultural traditions, such as certain Catholic and Orthodox customs, that favour an open casket as part of the liturgy.
- Confidence that presentation will be dignified and true to how the person looked in life.

The same research found that extended or specially cooled viewing rooms can be particularly valuable for parents grieving an infant, offering a gentler, less clinical setting for that final time together.

**Pro Tip:** *Ask your funeral director to see the deceased privately before the public viewing begins, so you know what to expect and can decide if changes are needed.*

## What a closed casket service involves and what to expect

A closed casket service means the coffin remains shut throughout the visitation, funeral Mass, or memorial, whether the body is present or not. Some families choose a memorial service with no body present at all, particularly after cremation has already taken place. A closed casket does not mean a lesser farewell: the coffin can still be central to the service, surrounded by flowers, photographs, and personal tributes.

This option often suits families who value privacy or who simply feel that a closed casket is a more dignified way to honour their loved one. It also tends to simplify logistics around cremation timing, since a closed casket allows the service to proceed on schedule without waiting on additional preparation for viewing.

- Coffin present, closed throughout the service and committal.
- Memorial or funeral Mass held after cremation, with no coffin present.
- A brief closed viewing for identification purposes only, without a public display.

## Why some families choose a closed casket

For many families, a closed casket is the kinder, more practical choice, particularly when protecting children or other vulnerable mourners from a confronting image. Illness, injury, or the effects of time since death can leave a body's condition unsuitable for viewing, and a skilled funeral director will say so plainly rather than let a family discover this on the day.

Some families also simply prefer privacy, wanting to remember their loved one as they were in life rather than through a final image. Others follow specific religious or personal customs that favour a closed casket as the more modest and dignified option.

- Protecting children or trauma-sensitive relatives from unnecessary distress.
- Respecting a body's condition when viewing would cause more harm than comfort.
- Honouring personal, cultural, or religious preferences for privacy and modesty.

## Decision checklist: questions and factors to guide your choice

Start with the deceased's own wishes if they left instructions, and confirm who holds legal authority to make funeral decisions if they did not. From there, work through the practical and emotional factors together as a family.

1. Did the deceased express a preference for burial, cremation, or a particular type of service?
2. Who has legal authority to make the final decision if wishes were not documented?
3. What is the body's current condition, and would embalming or refrigeration change what is possible?
4. Are there religious or cultural expectations that shape whether viewing is expected?
5. Are children or vulnerable relatives attending, and would they benefit from a private viewing instead of a public one?
6. Are there coronial or forensic factors that might limit viewing, as can happen in cases referred to [Coronial Services](https://coroners.nsw.gov.au/the-coronial-process/first-steps/viewing-the-deceased.html)?
7. What are the cost implications of embalming, extended viewing times, or a particular coffin type?
8. Would a partial viewing or private family time meet everyone's needs better than a full public viewing?

Remember that [a viewing is never a legal requirement in Australia](https://funeralsaustralia.org.au/arranging-funeral/); it remains a personal choice, not an obligation.

**Pro Tip:** *If family members disagree, ask your funeral director to arrange a short private viewing first. It often settles the question without conflict.*

## Preparing the body, preparing mourners, and considering alternatives

Once you have settled on open, closed, or something in between, a few practical steps make the day easier for everyone involved.

- Discuss embalming honestly with your funeral director, including cost and whether it is necessary for your circumstances.
- Choose clothing and personal items in advance so preparation can happen without last-minute decisions.
- Consider a partial viewing, such as seeing only the face and hands, or private family time before the public service.
- Prepare children with simple, honest, age-appropriate explanations of what they will see before they arrive.
- Check timing early: coronial cases can limit when a viewing is possible, and viewings are generally arranged by appointment.

A [funeral director's usual tasks](https://www.sl.nsw.gov.au/find-legal-answers/books-online/rest-assured-legal-guide-wills-estates-planning-ahead-and-funerals/arranging-funeral) include collecting paperwork, arranging transport, and supplying the coffin, and a good director will also explain exactly what you and your family will see and when.

## Expert guidance from Bruce Missen and Willow Tree Funerals

Bruce Missen's approach is simple: always offer families a choice, explain what presentation will involve in plain language, and never pressure anyone towards a viewing they are not ready for. At Willow Tree Funerals, that means private viewings arranged around what each family needs, honest guidance on embalming, and coordination of Catholic and multi-faith requirements where the liturgy calls for an open casket. Some families ask for a brief private moment before a public viewing; others choose a closed casket throughout and find that just as meaningful. Both are common, and both are respected.

![Expert guidance from Bruce Missen and Willow Tree Funerals — overview diagram](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790359432044_Expert-guidance-from-Bruce-Missen-and-Willow-Tree-Funerals-overview-diagram.jpeg)

## A director's perspective on making this choice

There is no wrong answer here, only the right answer for your family. I have sat with families who found deep peace in a final look, and others who found the same idea unbearable and chose closed, with no less love in the room. If you are unsure, call and talk it through before deciding anything.

> *— Bruce Missen*

## How Willow Tree Funerals can help

Whichever path feels right, Willow Tree Funerals will guide you through it without pressure or upsell. We coordinate private viewings, offer honest embalming guidance, and support Catholic and multi-faith services alongside secular ceremonies.

[![Willow Tree Funerals](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1780021199999_willowtreefunerals.jpg)](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/)

- Transparent [pricing](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/pricing) published upfront, with no hidden extras.
- Direct access to the funeral director, 24 hours a day, for a confidential conversation.
- [Pre-arranged funerals](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services/pre-arranged-funerals) that lock in today's arrangements for peace of mind later.

Call 02 8776 1667 or visit our [pricing page](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/pricing) to talk through what suits your family.

## Sources

For further reading, see Funerals Australia, Coronial Services NSW, and the [CCNSW factsheet on coffin options](https://www.cemeteries.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-01/CCNSW-Factsheet-3-Did-you-know.pdf). For guidance on money worries during bereavement, this [grief and financial decisions guide](https://teneishaecoleman.com/how-to-manage-grief-and-money-decisions-after-loss) may help.

This article is general information, not a substitute for advice from a qualified doctor. Consult a qualified healthcare professional about your own circumstances before acting on anything here.

- [Arranging - Funerals Australia](https://funeralsaustralia.org.au/arranging-funeral/)
- [Arranging a funeral | State Library of New South Wales (Rest Assured legal guide)](https://www.sl.nsw.gov.au/find-legal-answers/books-online/rest-assured-legal-guide-wills-estates-planning-ahead-and-funerals/arranging-funeral)
- [Viewing the deceased | Coronial Services NSW](https://coroners.nsw.gov.au/the-coronial-process/first-steps/viewing-the-deceased.html)
- [Qualitative research on family experiences of viewing (Australian study)](https://opus.lib.uts.edu.au/bitstream/10453/148325/2/IJPN-S-21-00042%20%281%29%20%281%29%20Submitted.pdf)

## FAQ

### Is it better to have a closed casket or open casket?

Neither is inherently better: the right choice depends on the family's needs, the deceased's wishes, and the body's condition. Viewings are optional under Australian funeral practice, chosen for personal, cultural, or religious reasons rather than required by law.

### Are open casket funerals traumatising?

For some mourners, viewing can be distressing, while for others it supports grieving and memory making; research into family experiences found responses vary significantly between individuals. Offering informed choice, rather than assuming one approach suits everyone, matters more than the format itself.

### Can you have an open casket some weeks after death?

Viewing timing depends heavily on preservation methods and any coronial involvement in the case. Speak with your funeral director early, since coronial cases can restrict or delay viewing and viewings are generally arranged by appointment.

### Does embalming affect whether an open casket is possible?

Embalming is often chosen to improve presentation for an open viewing but is not required in most circumstances under NSW rules, aside from specific cases such as mausoleum entombment or interstate and overseas transport. Ask your funeral director whether it is necessary for your family's situation before agreeing to it.

title: Child Funeral Support in NSW: Exact Documents and Questions to Ask
excerpt: Practical, NSW-specific steps for arranging a child's funeral: who to call, the exact documents you'll need, coronial timing, and the pricing questions to...
content:
![Funeral director reviewing paperwork with family member](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790437954382_Funeral-director-reviewing-paperwork-with-family-member.jpeg)

A funeral director arranges and manages the practical and legal steps for a child's funeral in New South Wales, from collection of the child to the final service. If your family is facing this, your immediate actions are to choose a director, authorise collection, confirm whether the death is a coronial matter, and ask for an [itemised written quote](https://www.nsw.gov.au/legal-and-justice/consumer-rights-and-protection/services/a-guide-to-arranging-a-funeral). These steps follow NSW Government and ACCC guidance and protect you from confusion at a time when clarity matters most.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - Families should request an itemised, written quote showing the minimum essential-service price before discussing any extras to ensure clear comparison and avoid hidden costs.
> - When a child's death is connected to sudden, unexplained circumstances, or reports to the Coroner are required, delays are likely until official release documentation is obtained.
> - The funeral director handles all paperwork, bookings, and liaises with authorities, but families must quickly identify if the death involves the Coroner to prevent delays.
> - Key documents include the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death, cremation permit if applicable, and hospital's Authority to Collect Deceased, especially for stillbirths and neonatal deaths.
> - Contacting a funeral director immediately after a death is essential, as they can verify legal requirements, provide clear guidance, and prepare provisional arrangements to ensure a smooth process.

***

## Table of Contents

- [What a funeral director will do and the decisions you make first](#what-a-funeral-director-will-do-and-the-decisions-you-make-first)
- [NSW legal, coronial and hospital procedures that affect timing](#nsw-legal-coronial-and-hospital-procedures-that-affect-timing)
- [Pricing, quotes and consumer rights in NSW](#pricing-quotes-and-consumer-rights-in-nsw)
- [Choosing the ceremony and ways to hold onto memories](#choosing-the-ceremony-and-ways-to-hold-onto-memories)
- [How Willow Tree Funerals supports families across NSW](#how-willow-tree-funerals-supports-families-across-nsw)
- [What families get wrong when planning a child's funeral](#what-families-get-wrong-when-planning-a-childs-funeral)
- [If you need help now, here's what happens when you call](#if-you-need-help-now-heres-what-happens-when-you-call)
- [Sources](#sources)
- [FAQ](#faq)

## What a funeral director will do and the decisions you make first

Once you contact a funeral director, the sequence of events becomes theirs to manage, though several decisions will still need your input early on. The director takes on the paperwork, logistics, and coordination with the hospital or coroner, while you focus on your family.

1. **Authorisation to collect.** The hospital issues an Authority to Collect Deceased form, and the funeral director completes this when collecting your child from the hospital mortuary.
2. **Time with your child.** Hospital social workers or, where relevant, Aboriginal Health Liaison Officers can support you to spend time with your child before collection.
3. **Bookings and notices.** The director arranges the cemetery or crematorium booking, transport, death notices and registration of the death.
4. **Information the director will ask for.** Expect questions about your preferred cemetery or crematorium, whether you want a religious or secular service, dates that suit extended family, and whether the death has been reported to the Coroner.

Most directors, including [Willow Tree Funerals](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/blog/how-to-compare-funeral-directors-before-need-nsw-guide), will talk you through this sequence on the first phone call, so you are never left guessing what happens next.

## NSW legal, coronial and hospital procedures that affect timing

Some child deaths in NSW must be reported to the Coroner, and this can affect how quickly a burial or cremation can proceed. Sudden or unexplained deaths, deaths involving accidents, and certain cases connected to child protection are the kinds of circumstances that trigger reporting, and [hospital and coroner guidance](https://resources.schn.health.nsw.gov.au/policies/policies/pdf/2006-8059.pdf) make clear that burials and cremations cannot go ahead until the Coroner or a medical referee releases the child.

A funeral director cannot rush this process, but they can prepare a provisional booking and keep you informed of the likely timeline while release documentation is finalised.

The documents involved in a straightforward case include:

- A Medical Certificate of Cause of Death, issued by the treating doctor or hospital.
- A cremation permit, where cremation is chosen, signed off by a medical referee.
- Perinatal forms, for a stillbirth or death shortly after birth.
- The hospital's Authority to Collect Deceased, which the funeral director completes on collection.

Stillbirths and neonatal deaths carry their own specific rules. NSW Government guidance confirms that hospital mortuary staff support memory-making and viewing before the funeral director takes over, and that the same Authority to Collect Deceased form applies. Your funeral director will liaise directly with Coronial Services or the relevant health unit so you are not the one chasing paperwork.

## Pricing, quotes and consumer rights in NSW

Every family deserves a clear, written quote before agreeing to anything, and this is a right, not a favour. The [ACCC's guidance on funeral services](https://www.accc.gov.au/consumers/specific-products-and-activities/funeral-services) sets out exactly what to ask for.

- Request an itemised written quote that lists essential services, disbursements such as cemetery or crematorium fees, and GST separately.
- Ask for the minimum essential-service price on its own, then a separate price for any preferred additions or ceremony elements.
- Confirm which charges are unavoidable, such as cemetery, crematorium and permit fees, and which are optional, such as flowers, a memorial video or livestreaming.
- Check the contract for the total price displayed up front, the payment terms, any late fees, and whether the clauses feel fair and clearly written.

Our own breakdown of [funeral price lists in Sydney](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/blog/funeral-price-list-whats-included-in-sydney#what-does-a-funeral-price-list-have-to-include-in-sydney) explains what should appear on a compliant quote, and our guide to [understanding funeral costs](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/blog/understanding-funeral-costs-sydney) walks through typical cost components.

**Pro Tip:** *Get the minimum essential-service price in writing before discussing any extras. It gives you a clean baseline to compare against any other quote.*

## Choosing the ceremony and ways to hold onto memories

Burial and cremation both remain available for a child's funeral in NSW, and the right choice depends on your family's faith, culture and what feels right rather than any rule. Burial involves a permit and a plot, whether at a family grave or a dedicated children's section, while cremation requires a medical referee's permit and gives you flexibility on timing for a later memorial.

- Catholic families often choose a requiem Mass, and a funeral director experienced with parish priests, such as through [Catholic funeral services](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services/catholic-funerals), can coordinate the liturgy alongside the practical arrangements.
- Secular families may prefer a celebrant-led service that reflects the child's personality without religious structure.
- Memory-making options, including handprints, footprints, a memorial video tribute or live streaming for family who cannot attend in person, can be arranged alongside the service, though each adds its own timing and cost.
- Venue and accessibility matter too. Extended family, cultural mourning practices and travel distances often shape whether a service suits a church, a chapel or a graveside setting.

Our [burial services page](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services/burial) sets out cemetery bookings and logistics in more detail for families weighing this decision.

## How Willow Tree Funerals supports families across NSW

Willow Tree Funerals was founded in 2018 and offers availability 24 hours a day to provide direct communication without a call centre. That direct access matters most in the hours after a child has died, when every question needs a straight answer.

- The funeral service serves families across greater Sydney, the Sutherland Shire, South West Sydney, Western Sydney, the Inner West, the North Shore, Wollongong, the Illawarra and the Central Coast.
- The service offers experience with Catholic requiem Masses and multi-faith services, working directly with parish priests.
- Pricing may be published online in an itemised manner rather than held back until a family is already committed.
- Practical support extends to handling collection permissions, [repatriation](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services) for families needing to move a child interstate or internationally, and memorial video or livestreaming for relatives who cannot be there in person.

**Willow Tree Funerals holds a five-star average across [47+ Google reviews](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au)** from families across its service area, a reflection of the trust built through direct, transparent arrangements rather than a call centre process.

## What families get wrong when planning a child's funeral

The advice most families receive focuses on choosing between burial and cremation, or between a religious and secular service. Those choices matter, but they are not where families lose time or money. The real risk sits in the paperwork: not knowing whether a death is a coronial matter, or not asking for the minimum essential-service price in writing before anything else is discussed.

![What families get wrong when planning a child's funeral — overview diagram](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790438024420_What-families-get-wrong-when-planning-a-child-s-funeral-overview-diagram.jpeg)

Conventional advice also tends to treat the funeral director as someone you engage after the practical questions are settled. In reality, the right director should be the first call you make, because they can tell you immediately whether the Coroner is involved, what the hospital still needs from you, and what a fair quote looks like.

If there is one thing to prioritise, it is this: ask for everything in writing before you agree to anything, and choose a director who will explain, plainly, what is required by law and what is a choice. That single habit protects a grieving family from confusion far more than any checklist of ceremony options ever will.

> *— Bruce Missen*

## If you need help now, here's what happens when you call

If you are facing this today, call a funeral director directly. Have the hospital's name, whether the Coroner has been mentioned, and any early thoughts on burial or cremation ready, though none of this needs to be settled before you call.

[![Willow Tree Funerals](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1780021199999_willowtreefunerals.jpg)](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/)

On that first call, we will confirm the authority to collect your child, walk you through an itemised written quote, and put a provisional booking in place so nothing is rushed. You can view our published packages on the [pricing page](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/pricing), our Catholic funeral services, or our [pre-arranged funerals](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services/pre-arranged-funerals) option if you are planning ahead for another family member. Bruce answers the phone himself, day or night.

## Sources

- [A guide to arranging a funeral | NSW Government](https://www.nsw.gov.au/legal-and-justice/consumer-rights-and-protection/services/a-guide-to-arranging-a-funeral)
- [Funeral services | ACCC](https://www.accc.gov.au/consumers/specific-products-and-activities/funeral-services)
- [SCHN policy: Management of death of a child in hospital](https://resources.schn.health.nsw.gov.au/policies/policies/pdf/2006-8059.pdf)

## FAQ

### Who arranges a child's funeral in NSW?

A funeral director arranges and manages a child's funeral in NSW, including collection from hospital, coronial liaison where needed, and all bookings and paperwork. Families choose the director, and the director handles the practical and legal steps from there.

### What documents are needed for a child's funeral in NSW?

Families typically need a Medical Certificate of Cause of Death, a cremation permit if cremation is chosen, and the hospital's Authority to Collect Deceased form. Stillbirths and neonatal deaths also require specific perinatal forms.

### Does every child's death get reported to the Coroner?

No, only certain circumstances trigger a coronial report, such as sudden or unexplained deaths, accidents, or cases connected to child protection. When a death is a coronial matter, burial or cremation cannot proceed until the Coroner or a medical referee releases the child.

### What should be included in a funeral quote in NSW?

A compliant quote lists essential services, disbursements such as cemetery or crematorium fees, and GST separately, with the minimum essential-service price shown on its own. The ACCC recommends getting this in writing before agreeing to any optional extras.

### Can a funeral director help with a stillbirth or newborn loss?

Yes, funeral directors experienced with stillbirth and neonatal loss work alongside hospital mortuary staff to complete the required forms and arrange a service that suits the family. Hospital staff can support memory-making and viewing before the funeral director takes over collection and arrangements.

title: Before You Send Funeral Flowers in Australia: Church & Council Rules
excerpt: Australian funeral flower etiquette: when and where to send blooms, church and council rules, safety notes and practical tips from a funeral director.
content:
![Modest funeral flowers beside church altar](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790569388719_Modest-funeral-flowers-beside-church-altar.jpeg)

Yes, flowers are a thoughtful and widely accepted way to express sympathy in Australia, but always check the funeral notice or ask the family first. Start there: if the notice says nothing, a phone call to a close relative or the funeral director will tell you what is welcome. A simple white bouquet sent to the family home is rarely wrong. When flowers are not wanted, a donation, a meal or an offer of practical help says the same thing in a different form.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - Sending flowers is generally acceptable, but always confirm the family's preferences by checking the funeral notice or asking someone close to the family.
> - Flowers are typically placed near the coffin or at the front of the chapel, with arrangements like sprays, wreaths, or posies suitable for different moments.
> - Common flowers such as lilies, white roses, and Australian natives carry specific mourning meanings and should be chosen with cultural and religious considerations in mind.
> - Delivery must be timed to arrive before the service starts, and cards should include your full name, relationship, and a brief, heartfelt message.
> - Checking cultural or faith-specific practices, cemetery rules, and requesting direct coordination with funeral staff ensure respectful, appropriate tributes.

***

## Table of Contents

- [The role of flowers at a funeral in Australia](#the-role-of-flowers-at-a-funeral-in-australia)
- [Common funeral arrangements and where to send them](#common-funeral-arrangements-and-where-to-send-them)
- [The language of flowers: popular blooms and colour symbolism in Australia](#the-language-of-flowers-popular-blooms-and-colour-symbolism-in-australia)
- [Practical etiquette: timing, delivery addresses and what to write on the sympathy card](#practical-etiquette-timing-delivery-addresses-and-what-to-write-on-the-sympathy-card)
- [Faiths, cultures and local communities: what to check before you send flowers](#faiths-cultures-and-local-communities-what-to-check-before-you-send-flowers)
- [Cemeteries, council rules and sustainability considerations](#cemeteries-council-rules-and-sustainability-considerations)
- [A funeral director's perspective: practical coordination and what families value](#a-funeral-directors-perspective-practical-coordination-and-what-families-value)
- [What Australians get wrong about funeral flowers](#what-australians-get-wrong-about-funeral-flowers)
- [Coordinating flowers as part of a Willow Tree Funerals service](#coordinating-flowers-as-part-of-a-willow-tree-funerals-service)
- [Sources](#sources)
- [FAQ](#faq)

## The role of flowers at a funeral in Australia

Flowers have long served as a quiet symbol of life, memory and consolation at Australian funerals. They soften the formality of a service and give mourners something to look at, touch and place, which matters when words feel inadequate. At the chapel or church, flowers typically appear on or beside the coffin and in small displays at the front, while at the family home they offer ongoing comfort in the days that follow.

There is a balance to strike, though. In Catholic funerals, [liturgical guidance](https://art.catholic.org.au/2022/10/19/honouring-gods-creation/) recommends moderation in floral decoration at Mass, favouring one or two tasteful arrangements over an altar crowded with tributes. Flowers are meant to accompany the ceremony, not compete with it. Willow Tree Funerals coordinates this placement with parish priests as a matter of course when planning a [Catholic funeral mass](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/blog/how-to-plan-catholic-funeral-sydney), so families are never left guessing what the church will allow.

## Common funeral arrangements and where to send them

Different arrangements suit different moments in the funeral, and knowing the difference helps your gesture land where it is meant to.

- **Casket sprays** sit directly on the coffin and are usually arranged by the immediate family or ordered through the funeral director.
- **Standing sprays and wreaths** are placed at the front of the chapel or beside the coffin, and suit friends, colleagues or extended family.
- **Posies and boxed arrangements** are smaller, informal gestures well suited to a family home rather than the service itself.
- **Potted plants** offer a lasting alternative to cut flowers and often end up planted in a family garden as an ongoing memorial.

Service-bound flowers need to arrive before the ceremony starts, since chapel staff have little time to arrange late deliveries once mourners are seated. A sympathy posy for the home carries no such deadline and can be sent any time, including weeks afterwards. When a notice reads "family flowers only," it means the immediate family has arranged the coffin flowers themselves and would prefer other mourners to consider a donation, a card or a small gesture to the home instead of a matching floral tribute.

## The language of flowers: popular blooms and colour symbolism in Australia

Certain flowers carry meanings that Australians have come to associate with mourning and remembrance, and choosing with those meanings in mind shows care.

- **Lilies** are linked with peace and resurrection, making them common in both Christian and secular services.
- **White roses** signal reverence and respect, one of the safest choices when you are unsure of the family's wishes.
- **Chrysanthemums** carry strong mourning associations in some cultures, particularly across parts of Europe and Asia, so they are worth checking before sending internationally or to multicultural families.
- **Carnations** are a modest, affordable way to convey respect.
- **Australian native flowers**, such as waratahs, banksias or kangaroo paws, offer a distinctly local alternative that connects the tribute to place.

White remains the [most standard mourning colour](https://www.smct.org.au/blog/popular-flower-arrangements-for-funerals) in Australian funeral flowers, though personal colours are increasingly used when they reflect the person's favourite shade, football team or personality.

**Worth knowing:** if the household has a cat, certain lilies can be harmful to pets, so it is worth asking your florist for a pet-safe substitute before ordering. Consider durability and biodegradability too. A hardy arrangement that lasts the week honours the family without adding to landfill once it fades.

## Practical etiquette: timing, delivery addresses and what to write on the sympathy card

Getting the timing and wording right turns a floral tribute from a nice gesture into a genuinely comforting one.

- **Service deliveries** need to arrive before the ceremony begins, addressed to the venue with the deceased's name and service time clearly marked.
- **Home deliveries** can happen any time, and a bunch arriving a week or two after the funeral, once the house has gone quiet, is often deeply appreciated.
- **Card wording** should include your full name and your relationship to the deceased or the family, since grieving families often cannot recall who sent what without that detail.

Keep the message short and sincere. For an acquaintance or colleague, "Thinking of you and your family at this difficult time" is enough. For a close friend, something more personal such as "[Name] meant so much to so many of us, and we will miss them dearly" fits better. For immediate family, a brief handwritten note referencing a specific memory carries more weight than a generic verse.

When a notice requests donations "in lieu of flowers," honour that request by giving to the nominated charity rather than sending blooms anyway. If the notice is unclear or silent on the matter, phoning the funeral director or a family member removes any guesswork.

**Pro Tip:** *If you are unsure whether flowers, a donation or both are appropriate, a two-minute call to the funeral home almost always settles it faster than searching online.*

## Faiths, cultures and local communities: what to check before you send flowers

Australia's religious make-up is genuinely mixed, and the [2021 Census](https://www.abs.gov.au/media-centre/media-releases/2021-census-shows-changes-australias-religious-diversity) recorded rising numbers of people identifying with no religion alongside continuing diversity across Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist and other faiths. That mix is exactly why checking before you send matters more in Australia than in a more religiously uniform country.

- **Christian services**, including Catholic funerals, generally welcome flowers, though moderation is preferred at the altar itself.
- **Jewish funerals and shiva houses** typically do not include flowers at all; [a donation in the person's memory is the customary alternative](https://lilysflorist.com.au/blog/a/understanding-sympathy-vs-funeral-flowers/).
- **Muslim funerals** are usually simple and swift, and many families [prefer donations or food over floral tributes](https://lilysflorist.com.au/blog/a/understanding-sympathy-vs-funeral-flowers/) at the mosque.
- **Hindu and Buddhist services** often incorporate flowers as part of the ritual itself, though styles and colours vary by community and region.
- **Chinese and Vietnamese Australian families** frequently favour white or yellow chrysanthemums, reflecting mourning traditions carried from their countries of origin.
- **Indigenous Australian protocols** vary widely between communities, so the respectful approach is to listen to the family or local elders and consider native plants where that feels appropriate.

## Cemeteries, council rules and sustainability considerations

Cemetery and council rules often catch visitors off guard, and it pays to check before you spend money on an elaborate tribute. Many NSW cemeteries, including those covered by policies such as [Hilltops Council's cemetery management policy](https://www.hilltops.nsw.gov.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Hilltops-Cemetery-Management-Policy-adopted-28-May-2025.pdf), restrict vase types to council-supplied or non-breakable options and will remove tributes once they deteriorate, to keep the grounds tidy and safe.

![Hands removing plastic from cemetery flowers](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790569391784_Hands-removing-plastic-from-cemetery-flowers.jpeg)

Before leaving a graveside tribute, remove plastic wrapping, rubber bands and cellophane, since these do not break down and grounds staff otherwise have to strip them off by hand. Fresh, biodegradable flowers are generally preferred over artificial ones, which many cemeteries remove during routine maintenance. If in doubt, a quick check of the specific cemetery's website or a call to its office will confirm what is allowed before you order.

## A funeral director's perspective: practical coordination and what families value

Some funeral directors personally coordinate floral arrangements for every family they serve, rather than passing the task to a call centre. Florists and funeral directors need a handful of details to avoid delivery errors: the service time and venue, whether the coffin or altar has size or placement restrictions, and any family preferences on colour or style. A short checklist covering these points before you order saves confusion on the day, particularly for Catholic services where altar space is limited.

![Funeral flower ordering coordination checklist](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790569402081_Funeral-flower-ordering-coordination-checklist.jpeg)

## What Australians get wrong about funeral flowers

The most common mistake is treating flower etiquette as a fixed set of rules rather than a question to ask. Australians increasingly assume white lilies are always safe, but that assumption breaks down the moment the family is Jewish, Muslim or simply prefers donations. The conventional advice, send flowers as a default gesture of sympathy, undersells how much variation exists between faiths, cultures and even individual families within the same faith.

What the research behind this guide actually supports is simpler than most etiquette columns suggest: check the notice, make one phone call if it is unclear, and let the family's stated wishes override whatever feels traditional. A donation given because it was requested means more than a bouquet given out of habit. If you prioritise one thing, prioritise that conversation over the arrangement itself. The flowers matter less than the attention behind them.

> *— Bruce Missen*

## Coordinating flowers as part of a Willow Tree Funerals service

Certain funeral homes help families sort out floral arrangements as one part of arranging a full service, aiming to avoid guesswork on the day. A funeral director may answer calls personally and work directly with parish priests in areas served when a Catholic Requiem Mass requires particular care with altar space.

[![Willow Tree Funerals](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1780021199999_willowtreefunerals.jpg)](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/)

- **Floral arrangements** can be organised as part of your service, with pricing discussed openly and upfront.
- **Catholic funeral coordination** includes liaising with the parish on liturgical placement of flowers around the coffin and altar.
- **Graveside services** and burial arrangements can include tribute placement guidance suited to the specific cemetery.

If you are planning a service and want flowers handled properly alongside the ceremony, view our [pricing and service options](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/pricing) or call to talk through what your family needs.

## Sources

- [Popular flower arrangements for funerals (SMCT)](https://www.smct.org.au/blog/popular-flower-arrangements-for-funerals)
- [Hilltops cemetery management policy (Hilltops Council)](https://www.hilltops.nsw.gov.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Hilltops-Cemetery-Management-Policy-adopted-28-May-2025.pdf)
- [Honouring God’s creation (Catholic liturgical art)](https://art.catholic.org.au/2022/10/19/honouring-gods-creation/)
- [Sympathy vs Funeral Flowers: A guide to 11 faiths (Lily's Florist)](https://lilysflorist.com.au/blog/a/understanding-sympathy-vs-funeral-flowers/)

## FAQ

### Whose name do you put on funeral flowers?

Include your full name and your relationship to the deceased or the family, such as "colleague" or "family friend," so the family can identify the sender later. Grieving families often review cards well after the funeral, when memory of who sent what has faded.

### What is the 3:5:8 rule for flowers?

This is a floristry design guideline for arranging odd numbers of stems to create visually balanced bouquets. It is a design convention used by florists rather than a rule of funeral etiquette, and it does not affect which flowers are appropriate to send.

### Do you bring flowers to a funeral in Australia?

Bringing a small bunch to the service is acceptable, but most flowers are better sent ahead to the venue before the ceremony starts or delivered separately to the family home. Always check the funeral notice first, since many Australian families now request donations or "family flowers only" instead.

### What is the proper etiquette for giving funeral flowers to family members?

Check the notice or ask a close relative or the funeral director whether flowers are welcome, since faith and personal preference both affect the answer. If flowers are appropriate, a simple, tasteful arrangement sent to the home with a short, sincere card is rarely the wrong choice.

title: Carry ashes from Australia: bring the death certificate
excerpt: A practical Australia first handbook for families carrying cremated ashes overseas. Clear steps on required documents, airline and biosecurity rules, and...
content:
![Traveller carrying ashes through airport](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790688483753_Traveller-carrying-ashes-through-airport.jpeg)

Yes, in most cases you can take cremated ashes out of Australia, but you must carry the right documents and follow both airline and destination country rules. Australia places no general export ban on cremated remains, though airlines require sealed containers and biosecurity officers pay close attention to urn materials. Before you travel, gather the death certificate and a crematorium letter, and confirm the specific requirements with your airline.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - Carrying cremated ashes out of Australia typically requires a death certificate, crematorium letter, and proof of only ashes in sealed, non-wooden containers.
> - Most airlines prefer that urns be in carry-on luggage, made of ceramic, metal, or sealed plastic, with documentation easily accessible during security checks.
> - Ashes are exempt from powder and liquid restrictions, but containers contaminated with soil or plant material must be declared and may be inspected on arrival.
> - Destination and transit country rules may differ from Australian requirements, so verifying requirements with consulates and airlines before travel is essential.
> - Engaging a funeral director early simplifies paperwork, logistics, and coordination for international repatriation, reducing delays and mishaps at departure.

***

## Table of Contents

- [Documents and paperwork to prepare before you fly](#documents-and-paperwork-to-prepare-before-you-fly)
- [Airline rules for carrying ashes on board or as checked baggage](#airline-rules-for-carrying-ashes-on-board-or-as-checked-baggage)
- [Biosecurity rules that affect the urn and its contents](#biosecurity-rules-that-affect-the-urn-and-its-contents)
- [Checking transit and destination rules before you travel](#checking-transit-and-destination-rules-before-you-travel)
- [Carrying ashes yourself versus arranging professional repatriation](#carrying-ashes-yourself-versus-arranging-professional-repatriation)
- [What families often overlook when planning an overseas repatriation](#what-families-often-overlook-when-planning-an-overseas-repatriation)
- [How Willow Tree Funerals supports families sending ashes abroad](#how-willow-tree-funerals-supports-families-sending-ashes-abroad)
- [Sources](#sources)
- [FAQ](#faq)

## Documents and paperwork to prepare before you fly

Every family carrying ashes overseas should travel with certified proof of the cremation and the identity of the deceased. This paperwork rarely needs to be shown, but when it is requested, having it ready prevents delay and distress at an already difficult moment.

- A **certified death certificate**, obtained through NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages or the relevant state registry.
- A **crematorium letter** confirming the deceased's name, the date of cremation and the crematorium's contact details.
- **Certified translations** if your destination country does not use English, arranged through the consulate or a registered translator.

According to [NSW Health](http://health.nsw.gov.au/environment/factsheets/Pages/cremation-ashes.aspx), no public health unit approval is required to transport cremated ashes overseas from Australia, though carrying a death certificate and crematorium statement helps smooth interactions with airline staff and border officials. Many crematoria will also state explicitly, on request, that the urn contains only cremated remains with no foreign matter present, a line that often resolves questions on the spot.

**Pro Tip:** *Carry the originals, a photocopy in your check-in luggage, and a scanned copy on your phone, so you're never without proof if one set goes missing.*

## Airline rules for carrying ashes on board or as checked baggage

Most families are advised to keep the urn in hand luggage rather than checked baggage, simply because carry-on items stay under your control and avoid the rough handling that checked bags can receive. Airlines will X-ray the container as a matter of course, and staff may ask to see your documentation, though this is usually a brief check rather than a lengthy process.

- Choose a **sealed, leak-proof container** made of ceramic, metal or plastic.
- Avoid **wooden urns** where possible, since timber can trigger closer biosecurity scrutiny.
- Keep the crematorium letter and death certificate accessible, not buried in checked luggage.
- If the urn cannot travel as baggage, ask your funeral director about freight options.

**Cremated remains are specifically exempt from the powder and liquid restrictions applied to international carry-on baggage departing Australia**, according to [Qantas](https://www.qantas.com/en-at/baggage/carry-on), though normal carry-on weight limits still apply. Qantas notes that shipping remains as freight is treated as a "special movement", usually arranged through a funeral director working with [Qantas Freight](https://help.qantas.com/agencyconnect/s/article/Travelling-with-Ashes-cremated-remains-and-Coffins) rather than booked as ordinary cargo by the public.

## Biosecurity rules that affect the urn and its contents

Clean cremated remains carry no human biosecurity risk on their own. The concern lies with what might be attached to the urn or packed alongside it, particularly soil, plant matter or untreated timber.

- Choose **ceramic, metal or sealed plastic** containers over raw wood.
- Keep the urn free of soil, flowers or plant material from a scattering site.
- Declare the container on your **Incoming Passenger Card** if it contains any biosecurity risk material.
- Ask your crematorium to confirm in writing that the urn contains only ashes.

The [Department of Health](https://www.health.gov.au/topics/communicable-diseases/biosecurity/importing-human-remains?language=en) confirms there are no import permits or documentation requirements for clean cremated human remains from a biosecurity standpoint, but containers or ashes contaminated with soil or plant material must be declared and may be inspected on arrival to Australia.

**Pro Tip:** *If you're bringing ashes home to Australia after a scattering ceremony held overseas, wipe down the urn and avoid packing any soil or flowers with it.*

![Hands cleaning urn before air travel](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790688484275_Hands-cleaning-urn-before-air-travel.jpeg)

## Checking transit and destination rules before you travel

Australia's own rules are only half the picture. Transit airports and the destination country can each apply their own requirements, and there's no guarantee they'll match what applies at home.

1. Contact the **destination country's consulate or embassy** in Australia to confirm what documents and container types they accept.
2. Ask specifically whether a **permit** is needed to bring ashes into that country, since some do require one.
3. Check the **transit country's rules** separately if your flight stops en route, not just the final destination.
4. Use [Smartraveller](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/while-overseas/personal-emergencies/what-happens-if-someone-dies-overseas) for consular advice if the death occurred overseas and remains need to be returned to Australia.
5. Arrange **local funeral assistance at the destination** in advance if a scattering ceremony or service is planned there.

## Carrying ashes yourself versus arranging professional repatriation

For a straightforward trip with one urn and a cooperative airline, carrying the ashes yourself is usually the simpler and cheaper path. You keep direct control of the remains, avoid freight paperwork, and the trip proceeds on your own schedule.

Complex cases suit professional help better. A funeral director can manage documentation, liaise with overseas funeral homes, and handle freight bookings when a coronial matter, a large urn or a difficult destination is involved.

- **Carrying it yourself:** lower cost, faster, full personal control over the urn.
- **Using a funeral director or freight service:** professional handling of paperwork, coordination with airlines and overseas providers, better suited to coronial cases.

According to Smartraveller, repatriation involving coronial enquiries can take several weeks, since it depends on cooperation between local authorities, consulates and Australian funeral directors.

**Pro Tip:** *If a death has occurred overseas and repatriation is involved, engage a funeral director early. The paperwork chain is long, and starting it late is the single biggest cause of delay.*

## What families often overlook when planning an overseas repatriation

![What families often overlook when planning an overseas repatriation — overview diagram](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790688546416_What-families-often-overlook-when-planning-an-overseas-repatriation-overview-diagram.jpeg)

The families we speak with rarely underestimate the grief of the moment, but they often underestimate the paperwork. A crematorium letter requested the day before a flight, a wooden urn still holding scattering soil, or an assumption that a transit country's rules will mirror Australia's, these are the details that cause delay at the departure gate.

Engaging a funeral director early, well before travel dates are locked in, removes most of that risk. A director who has coordinated international transfers before knows which documents each consulate tends to ask for and which urn types travel without friction.

> *— Bruce Missen*

## How Willow Tree Funerals supports families sending ashes abroad

Willow Tree Funerals coordinates [repatriation](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services) for families across Sydney who need cremated remains handled correctly for international travel, from the crematorium letter through to liaison with overseas funeral homes. Arrangements are personally managed to ensure families speak directly with the coordinator rather than a call centre.

[![Willow Tree Funerals](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1780021199999_willowtreefunerals.jpg)](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/)

- We assist with preparing the death certificate and crematorium letter needed for airline and consulate checks.
- We provide advice on urn selection, focusing on materials that typically clear airport screening and biosecurity checks.
- We coordinate with overseas funeral homes and freight providers when special movement is required rather than passenger carriage.

Full [cremation and pricing details](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/pricing) are published on our site, and families considering repatriation are welcome to call 02 8776 1667 to talk through documentation and timing before booking flights.

## Sources

- [Importing human remains and biosecurity — Australian Government, Department of Health](https://www.health.gov.au/topics/communicable-diseases/biosecurity/importing-human-remains?language=en)
- [Cremation ashes fact sheet — NSW Health](http://health.nsw.gov.au/environment/factsheets/Pages/cremation-ashes.aspx)
- [Travelling with ashes, cremated remains and coffins — Qantas help](https://help.qantas.com/agencyconnect/s/article/Travelling-with-Ashes-cremated-remains-and-Coffins)
- [Qantas carry-on baggage restrictions — Qantas](https://www.qantas.com/en-at/baggage/carry-on)
- [If someone dies while travelling overseas — Smartraveller (DFAT)](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/while-overseas/personal-emergencies/what-happens-if-someone-dies-overseas)

## FAQ

### Do I need to declare ashes to customs when travelling?

You only need to declare cremated ashes on your Incoming Passenger Card if the container has soil, plant matter or is made of untreated wood, according to the Department of Health. Clean ashes in a sealed ceramic, metal or plastic urn generally don't need to be declared.

### Do I have to tell an airline if I'm travelling with someone's ashes?

Airlines generally expect you to carry ashes in a sealed, leak-proof container and to be ready for X-ray screening, though you don't usually need to notify them in advance for a single urn in carry-on baggage. Qantas treats shipping remains as freight differently, as a special movement arranged through a funeral director rather than standard baggage.

### How do you transport human ashes internationally?

Carry a certified death certificate and a crematorium letter, pack the ashes in a sealed non-wooden container, and check both airline and destination country rules before you fly. For coronial cases or larger repatriations, a funeral director typically coordinates the documentation and freight arrangements with overseas providers.

### Does Australia restrict exporting cremated ashes?

Australia places no general restriction on exporting cremated human remains, and no public health unit approval is required, according to NSW Health. Airlines and destination countries, rather than Australian export law, are usually the source of any extra requirements.

### What if the ashes are lost or delayed during transport?

Contact the airline immediately to trace checked baggage or freight, and keep your crematorium letter and death certificate on hand as proof of the shipment's contents. If a repatriation involving coronial processes is delayed, a funeral director can liaise with consular staff and the destination funeral home on your behalf.

title: Maronite Funerals Australia: Ginnaz, 40 Day Mourning & Planning
excerpt: Clear explainer of Maronite funerals in Australia: Book of Ginnaz rites, wake to graveside, the 40 day Geneze memorial and planning help.
content:
![Hands preparing incense for Maronite funeral](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790712389568_Hands-preparing-incense-for-Maronite-funeral.jpeg)

Maronite funeral traditions are a structured sequence of hymn-centred rites, moving from the wake through the church ginnaz to the graveside, framed by psalms, the Hoosoyo and sacred chant. Families can expect a two-stage funeral service followed by a 40-day mourning period, closed by the Geneze Memorial Mass, and later marked again at the one-year Mass.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - The funeral rites include three stages: the wake, the church ginnaz, and the graveside, each emphasizing hymnody and prayer to accompany the departed.
> - The ginnaz features a detailed liturgy with psalms, incense, scripture, and hymns, often retaining melodies across languages to preserve tradition.
> - The 40-day mourning period concludes with a Geneze Memorial Mass, followed by a one-year memorial, emphasizing ongoing prayer and remembrance.
> - Practical coordination with parish clergy and funeral directors is essential, including scheduling the ginnaz, graveside rites, and memorial masses, especially for families overseas.
> - Hymn melodies, especially in Syriac, are preserved in translation to Arabic and English, ensuring liturgical continuity and recognition across generations.

***

## Table of Contents

- [The structure and purpose of Maronite funeral rites](#the-structure-and-purpose-of-maronite-funeral-rites)
- [Wake and home rites: what happens before the church service](#wake-and-home-rites-what-happens-before-the-church-service)
- [The church ginnaz: structure, prayers and music](#the-church-ginnaz-structure-prayers-and-music)
- [Graveside rites and the final farewell](#graveside-rites-and-the-final-farewell)
- [Mourning timeline and memorials: 40 days, Geneze and the one-year Mass](#mourning-timeline-and-memorials-40-days-geneze-and-the-one-year-mass)
- [Practical guidance for families planning a Maronite funeral](#practical-guidance-for-families-planning-a-maronite-funeral)
- [Language, chant and local variations across Maronite communities](#language-chant-and-local-variations-across-maronite-communities)
- [Supporting Maronite families through unfamiliar rites](#supporting-maronite-families-through-unfamiliar-rites)
- [How Willow Tree Funerals supports Maronite families](#how-willow-tree-funerals-supports-maronite-families)
- [Where to find the prayers, hymns and official guidance](#where-to-find-the-prayers-hymns-and-official-guidance)
- [Sources](#sources)
- [FAQ](#faq)

## The structure and purpose of Maronite funeral rites

Maronite theology frames death as a passage, and the funeral rite as an act of accompaniment. The Church does not simply farewell the departed; it walks with them through prayer, incense and hymn toward the paschal hope of resurrection. This is why hymnody carries such weight throughout the service: the [Book of Ginnazat](https://www.sjmaronite.org/files/Ginnazat.pdf) describes hymns historically sung in procession, known as hymns of the road, as a central expressive element that accompanies the departed on their final journey.

The funeral unfolds across three connected stations, each with its own tone and purpose:

1. **The wake**, held at the family home or a funeral parlour, where the community gathers to pray, console and prepare for the church rite.
2. **The church ginnaz**, the formal funeral liturgy of psalms, readings, incense and chant, celebrated in the parish church.
3. **The graveside rite**, the final commendation and committal, where the body is laid to rest with blessing and prayer.

Modern parish life has shortened and adapted parts of this sequence, particularly through the use of vernacular language rather than historic Syriac. What has not changed is the priority given to hymnody itself: scholarship on Maronite liturgical reform notes that even where texts were translated or trimmed, the melodic tradition was deliberately preserved so that the sound of Maronite mourning remains recognisable across generations and parishes.

## Wake and home rites: what happens before the church service

The wake is where grief first becomes communal. Traditionally held in the family home, it is increasingly common today for the wake to take place at a funeral parlour, particularly in diaspora communities where family homes may not comfortably accommodate visitors. Either setting serves the same purpose: giving relatives, friends and parishioners a chance to view the deceased, offer condolences and pray together before the funeral liturgy.

The atmosphere is one of quiet hospitality rather than formality. Typical elements include:

- A viewing period where family and close friends sit with the deceased.
- Recitation of the rosary or short prayers led by a family member or visiting priest.
- Offering of tea, coffee or light refreshments to visitors as they arrive.
- A public announcement of the time and place for receiving condolences, so the wider community knows when to attend.

Families are usually the ones who decide how long the wake runs and who is invited to speak or pray. Behind the scenes, a funeral director coordinates the practical side: collecting the deceased, preparing the body, and arranging the transfer to church in good time for the ginnaz.

**Pro Tip:** *Ask your funeral director to confirm the wake's start and finish times with the parish office early, so the church booking and the home or parlour gathering do not clash.*

## The church ginnaz: structure, prayers and music

The ginnaz is the heart of a Maronite funeral, a structured liturgy built from psalms, scripture, incense and hymnody rather than a single continuous prayer. The Book of Ginnazat records this structure in detail, and it also organises separate ginnazat for different groups, including men, women and clergy, reflecting how precisely the tradition has been preserved over centuries.

A typical ginnaz moves through several recognisable stages:

- **Opening doxology**, praising God and setting the liturgical tone.
- **Psalmody**, drawing on key psalms associated with mercy and rest for the departed.
- **Hoosoyo**, the rite of incense and prayers of mercy, offered for the soul of the deceased.
- **Mazmooro**, a chanted response that punctuates the readings.
- **A reading from St Paul**, usually addressing resurrection and hope.
- **Fetgomo and Gospel**, a proclaimed passage that anchors the rite in scripture.
- **Bo'outo**, a penitential hymn form calling for mercy.
- **Concluding prayers**, commending the deceased to God before the coffin is prepared for procession.

A short glossary helps here, since these terms rarely appear outside Maronite worship. Ginnaz refers to the funeral rite itself. Hoosoyo is the prayer and incense of mercy offered for the departed. Mazmooro is a sung, responsorial element. Fetgomo introduces the Gospel reading, and bo'outo is a penitential hymn asking for God's compassion.

**The Book of Ginnazat sets out this structure of psalms, incense, scripture and hymnody as the fixed pattern of the funeral liturgy**, which is why parish practice, even when shortened, tends to retain each element in some form rather than omitting stages outright.

Music carries theological weight in the ginnaz. Hymns were historically chanted in Syriac, and where parishes have moved to Arabic or English texts, the melodies themselves are frequently retained, a deliberate choice documented in scholarship on Maronite liturgical reform, including the Kaslik and Aleppo editions. The sound of the chant, not only the words, carries the sense of continuity between generations.

Length and content vary by parish. Some priests incorporate a brief homily or personal reflection; formal eulogies, where offered, are usually placed outside the liturgy itself, before or after the ginnaz, at the discretion of the celebrant. The Mass itself may be celebrated as a full Requiem, or Qorbono, depending on the day and the family's wishes, and it is worth asking your parish which form applies before the day of the funeral.

## Graveside rites and the final farewell

The procession to the grave is not simply transport. It is understood as a continuation of the accompaniment that began at the wake, and hymns sung along the way, historically called hymns of the road, express that the community is still walking with the departed even as the body moves toward its resting place.

At the graveside, the rite is brief but deliberate:

1. The priest leads final prayers of commendation, asking for God's mercy on the soul of the deceased.
2. The coffin and the grave itself are blessed, often with holy water, before the body is lowered.
3. A short committal formula is spoken, entrusting the body to the earth in hope of resurrection.
4. Family members are frequently invited to place a handful of earth or a flower on the coffin as a personal farewell.

Some older customs, such as anointing at the graveside, have become less common in contemporary parish practice, though they persist in some communities depending on the priest and family preference. Families attending should expect the graveside portion to move at a measured pace: standing close but allowing the priest room to lead, and following the lead of immediate family when it comes to any physical gesture of farewell.

## Mourning timeline and memorials: 40 days, Geneze and the one-year Mass

Mourning does not end at the graveside. Maronite custom sets out a structured period of remembrance that continues for weeks and years after burial, giving families a clear rhythm for grief rather than leaving it open-ended.

- The **40-day mourning period** begins on the day of death and concludes with a dedicated **Geneze Memorial Mass**, a milestone [widely observed in Maronite and broader Lebanese practice](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/blog/lebanese-funeral-customs).
- A **one-year memorial Mass** is customary, marking the anniversary of death with a further liturgy and gathering.
- The Maronite liturgical calendar also sets aside **three weeks of commemoration**, dedicated in turn to priests, to the righteous and just, and to the faithful departed generally, reflecting the [Eparchy's pastoral emphasis](https://maronite.org.au/news/maronite-weeks-of-commemoration/) on continual prayer for the dead rather than a single annual remembrance.
- Praying for the departed is regarded pastorally as an act of mercy, since the dead can no longer pray for themselves, which is why parishes actively encourage families to request Masses beyond the standard milestones.

Arranging these memorial Masses is usually straightforward: contact the parish office, nominate the date and the name of the deceased for the Mass intention, and confirm whether the family wishes to gather afterwards. Families comparing timelines across denominations sometimes find it useful to look at how [other diaspora communities observe similar 40-day memorials](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/blog/greek-orthodox-40-day-memorial#what-happens-during-the-40-day-memorial-service), since the underlying rhythm of structured remembrance is shared even where the specific prayers differ.

## Practical guidance for families planning a Maronite funeral

Organising a Maronite funeral involves coordinating both the parish and a funeral director, and having a clear order of calls in the first hours makes a difficult day more manageable.

1. Contact the doctor or, where death was unexpected, the appropriate authorities, before anything else.
2. Call your parish priest to begin arranging the ginnaz and confirm available dates.
3. Contact your funeral director to arrange collection of the deceased and begin practical preparations.
4. Notify close family so decisions about the wake and condolence times can be made together.

When speaking with the parish, it helps to ask directly about the language of the readings and hymns, whether Syriac elements will be included, the proposed time for the Requiem or Qorbono, and how the parish typically schedules the 40-day and one-year memorial Masses.

Your funeral director can answer a parallel set of questions: how the removal and transport will be handled, what graveside logistics look like at your chosen cemetery, whether repatriation is needed if the deceased is to be buried overseas, and whether pre-arrangement is worth considering for future planning.

On the day itself, attendees generally wear dark, modest clothing, and it is common for families to nominate whether they prefer flowers or donations to a chosen cause. Condolence gatherings after the graveside rite, whether at a home or a hired venue, remain an important part of the mourning process rather than an optional add-on.

**Pro Tip:** *Write your questions for the parish and the funeral director down in one list before your first calls. Grief makes it easy to forget details that matter later, such as hymn language or memorial scheduling.*

## Language, chant and local variations across Maronite communities

Syriac was historically the liturgical language of the Maronite Church, and its chant forms remain the backbone of funeral hymnody even today. As communities shifted toward Arabic, and later English in diaspora parishes, scholarship on Maronite liturgical reform shows that translators worked to preserve the original melodies rather than composing entirely new settings, which is why a funeral chanted in English can still sound recognisably Maronite to someone familiar with the Syriac originals.

Parishes balance this heritage against the practical need for lay participation, particularly where a congregation includes several generations with differing language fluency. Families wanting specific Syriac hymns, a particular chant setting or a bilingual service should raise this with the parish's music minister well ahead of the funeral date, since not every cantor maintains the same repertoire. Being specific, naming a hymn or a moment in the liturgy where a particular chant matters to the family, gives the music minister the clearest brief to work from.

## Supporting Maronite families through unfamiliar rites

In more than seven years of arranging funerals across Sydney's Maronite and broader Lebanese communities, I have learned that families rarely need the tradition explained to them. What they need is someone who can coordinate the practical side without getting in the way of it.

That means liaising directly with the parish on timing, helping arrange music ministers when a family has a particular hymn in mind, keeping track of the 40-day and one-year Mass dates, and managing repatriation paperwork when a loved one is to be buried overseas. Respecting the rite means understanding it well enough to stay quietly out of its way, while still being available for every practical question a family has.

> *— Bruce Missen*

## How Willow Tree Funerals supports Maronite families

Coordinating a Maronite funeral means working closely with a parish priest, a music minister and a cemetery, often within a matter of days. Willow Tree Funerals handles that coordination directly, liaising with parish clergy across the areas we serve to confirm ginnaz timing, arrange graveside logistics, and organise memorial Mass scheduling for the 40-day and one-year observances.

[![Willow Tree Funerals](https://csuxjmfbwmkxiegfpljm.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-images/organization-6784/1780021199999_willowtreefunerals.jpg)](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/)

Our [Catholic Funerals](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services/catholic-funerals) service covers Requiem and Qorbono coordination for Maronite and other Eastern Catholic families, and we offer [graveside services](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services/graveside-services) for families who wish to hold a simpler committal. Where a loved one needs to be returned overseas for burial, our [repatriation](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services) service manages the international transfer of remains, and families who want to plan ahead can lock in today's arrangements through our [pre-arranged funerals](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/services/pre-arranged-funerals) option, with funds held in a regulated trust.

Every family speaks directly with Bruce Missen, the funeral director, day or night, never a call centre. Our pricing is published openly on our [pricing page](https://willowtreefunerals.com.au/pricing), so you know what a Catholic or Maronite funeral involves before you commit to anything. Call us on 02 8776 1667 to talk through the details of a Maronite funeral for your family.

![How Willow Tree Funerals supports Maronite families — overview diagram](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-6784/1790712450102_How-Willow-Tree-Funerals-supports-Maronite-families-overview-diagram.jpeg)

## Where to find the prayers, hymns and official guidance

Families wanting to read the liturgy itself can consult the Book of Ginnazat, which sets out the full structure of psalms, incense and hymns used in the ginnaz. The Maronite Eparchy's page on the weeks of commemoration explains the pastoral reasoning behind ongoing prayer for the departed, while research into Maronite chant and liturgical reform explains how the music has survived translation into Arabic and English. For practical, Australian-facing guidance on the mourning period itself, see our own article on Lebanese funeral customs.

## Sources

- [Book of Ginnazat (Ginnazat.pdf)](https://www.sjmaronite.org/files/Ginnazat.pdf)
- [Maronite weeks of commemoration | Maronite Eparchy](https://maronite.org.au/news/maronite-weeks-of-commemoration/)

## FAQ

### Why are eulogies not allowed at Catholic funerals?

Formal eulogies are generally kept outside the funeral Mass itself because the liturgy is centred on prayer and scripture rather than personal tribute. Many parishes instead allow a brief reflection before or after the Mass, or at the wake, so families can still share memories in a fitting setting.

### What is the tradition of 9 days after death?

Maronite tradition centres its structured mourning around a 40-day period rather than nine days, concluding with the Geneze Memorial Mass. Some other Christian and cultural traditions observe a nine-day cycle of prayer, but this is not the standard Maronite practice.

### Are Maronites closer to Catholics or Orthodox?

Maronites are Eastern Catholics, in full communion with Rome while retaining their own Syriac liturgical heritage and traditions. This places Maronite funeral practice within the Catholic Church, even though its rites, chants and calendar differ from the Roman Rite familiar to many Western Catholics.

### How many days after death is a Catholic funeral?

There is no fixed universal rule, and timing depends on the family, the parish and cemetery availability, though funerals commonly take place within about a week of death. Maronite families should confirm timing directly with their parish priest, since ginnaz scheduling depends on church availability and family circumstances.
